Russian Frigate Armed With Nuclear-Capable Zircons Appears Off German Coast With Tracker Switched Off
Russia has deployed one of its most advanced warships, armed with nuclear-capable Zircon hypersonic missiles, close to a German island in the Baltic Sea amid escalating Kremlin threats against British and European shipping, The Telegraph reported on August 17.
The Admiral Kasatonov, a modern Russian frigate capable of long-range strikes and anti-submarine warfare, was spotted last week near Fehmarn, a German island and popular tourist destination in the Baltic.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
According to The Telegraph, the frigate was sailing with its location transponder switched off, making its subsequent movements difficult to track. It remained unclear as of August 17 whether the ship was still operating near the island.
Commissioned in 2020, Admiral Kasatonov is considered one of the Russian Navy’s most modern surface combatants. Among its weapons are 3M22 Zircon hypersonic missiles, which Russia says can strike targets at long range and can be equipped with conventional or nuclear warheads.
The Telegraph described the deployment as the latest escalation between Russia and NATO in the Baltic, one of Europe’s most important maritime corridors and an increasingly tense arena for Russian and allied military activity.
Admiral Kasatonov is also the second Russian warship to appear in the Baltic in recent weeks. The destroyer Admiral Levchenko arrived in the region in late July.
The deployments come as Moscow increasingly threatens retaliation over Western actions against Russia’s so-called shadow fleet—a sprawling network of aging tankers and commercial vessels used to move Russian oil and other goods despite international sanctions.
Britain and France have intercepted or seized vessels suspected of operating for Russia in recent months, increasing pressure on the network Moscow relies on to sustain energy exports.
During an inspection of a Russian warship last week, Russian leader Vladimir Putin threatened reciprocal action against British and European vessels if Russia-linked ships were seized.
“It’s nothing but piracy and robbery. If this is done, we will be forced to respond in kind… [Russia can retaliate] in any area where we see it as necessary and appropriate,” Putin said.
He specifically mentioned the Pacific Ocean, a major route for British and European commercial shipping, where Russian officials have also discussed plans to board and inspect vessels.
Former Russian leader and current Security Council deputy chairman Dmitry Medvedev has issued even broader threats.
“Russia has the right to attack any merchant ship belonging to an enemy state, whether in our or neutral waters, if there is sufficient suspicion that it is transporting cargo in the interest of the enemy,” Medvedev said, referring to NATO states supporting Ukraine.
The arrival of the Zircon-armed frigate near Germany adds a military dimension to those threats.
Earlier, reports emerged that British warships and helicopters spent significantly more time tracking Russian naval activity in July as Moscow maintained an elevated presence around UK waters and across the North Atlantic.
Royal Navy patrol ships and aircraft devoted 21 days to monitoring Russian vessels during the month, up 25% from July 2025, according to figures released by the British Navy.
Discuss this article:

articles.title: Russia Has Started Supplying Explosives to Iran to Replenish Weapons Stocks
articles.body:
- Category
- World
Russia Has Started Supplying Explosives to Iran to Replenish Weapons Stocks
Russia has begun shipping explosives, ammunition, and drone parts across the Caspian Sea to help Iran replenish its missile and drone stocks following strikes by the US and Israel.
According to a European government document cited by NBC News on August 18, the maritime route allows both nations to transfer military cargo directly between Russian and Iranian ports.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
The landlocked Caspian Sea is bordered by five countries: Russia, Iran, Kazakhstan, Turkmenistan, and Azerbaijan. Because Western navies, including the US Navy, do not operate in these waters, they cannot interdict shipments moving between the two allies.
In late March, Israel targeted the Iranian port complex of Bandar Anzali on the Caspian coast. Israeli officials said the facility was used to transport weapons from Russia. Shipments through the port restarted shortly after the operation.
The reliance on this supply route highlights a growing strategic alliance between Moscow and Tehran. Iranian forces have used drones and missiles against US military bases in the Middle East, leading to the deaths of at least 18 American service members since the start of active hostilities.
During the early stages of Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine, Tehran provided primary support to Moscow. Iran supplied ready-to-use Shahed strike drones alongside production technology. Russian engineers later upgraded the design and established mass production inside Russia.
Reports from Financial Times previously indicated that Russia began sending drones back to Iran while sharing satellite imagery, intelligence, and targeting data to hit US positions in the Middle East.
US and Iranian officials agreed to a 60-day ceasefire in mid-June, which was extended for another two months in August. Reports from The Wall Street Journal state that Tehran is using this pause in fighting to rebuild its military inventory. Iranian officials aim to inflict sufficient damage on US and Israeli forces to deter future large-scale strikes on Iranian territory.
On July 25, 2026, Ukraine’s Security Service (SBU) launched long-range drone strikes against multiple Russian military and logistical targets, hitting air defense systems in Rostov-on-Don and naval assets in the Caspian Sea.
The SBU reported damaging a 92N6E radar tower, a Tor-M2 air defense system, an electronic warfare complex, and two FPV drone warehouses in Rostov-on-Don.
In the Caspian Sea, Ukrainian drones targeted the Filanovsky offshore oil platform alongside two sanctioned cargo ships, the Port Olya 2 and the Begey, which had been transporting Iranian military equipment and ammunition to Russia.
Additionally, Ukrainian forces struck a Russian Project 12418 Molniya-class missile boat stationed in the region.
In March 2026, Russia openly declared its support for Iran amid escalating confrontations involving the United States and Israel, signaling that Moscow did not consider itself a neutral actor in the Middle East crisis.
Russian Ambassador to the United Kingdom Andrei Kelin confirmed that Moscow was siding with Tehran, criticizing Western governments for placing full blame on Iran while ignoring initial strikes by the US and Israel.
Pointing to the deepening strategic partnership between the two nations since the start of Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine, Kelin called for an immediate end to hostilities and a return to political dialogue rather than military escalation.
Discuss this article:

articles.title: Trump’s slight of South Korea in favor of the North raises broader US security concerns
articles.body:
Trump’s slight of South Korea in favor of the North raises broader US security concerns
WASHINGTON (AP) — President Donald Trump’s decision to scale back joint military exercises with South Korea does not just slight a longtime ally but raises broader concerns about the security interests of the United States in Asia and elsewhere.
Trump explained his decision by citing South Korea’s refusal to join his war against Iran and pointing to what he said was his good relationship with North Korea’s reclusive dictator, a transactional and personal approach to foreign policy that has defined the Republican’s presidency.
“There is no American interest that I can see in this,” said Dan Fried, an assistant secretary of state for European affairs in the George W. Bush administration. “On all levels it makes no sense. It undermines the South Koreans, undermines the Japanese, frightens the Taiwanese, unnerves NATO and emboldens the Chinese, not to mention the North Koreans.”
Danny Russel, former assistant secretary of state for East Asia and the Pacific in the Obama administration, said Trump’s decision to side with North Korea, which strongly objects to the annual joint military exercises, is “firmly in the ‘hard-to see-how-it-could-be-worse’ category.”
“It is tragically upside-down. Trump is punishing an ally while encouraging an adversary,” said Russel, now a scholar at the Asia Society Policy Institute in New York. “He is protecting Kim Jong Un’s sensitive feelings from an unfriendly signal at the expense of U.S.-South Korean security.”
The message it sends to South Koreans
Trump on Sunday ordered the U.S. military to downsize the 11-day Ulchi Freedom Shield exercises, which began Monday as scheduled. It wasn’t known which parts of the training were being scaled back.
His announcement baffled many in South Korea, which has been closely allied with the U.S. for decades and where national security is a top priority due to threats from nuclear-armed North Korea.
It also drew instant criticism from many Democrats in Congress.
“Treating one of America’s closest allies like an adversary weakens our alliances and benefits China and North Korea,” said Rep. Greg Meeks of New York, the top Democrat on the House Foreign Affairs Committee, in a statement.
Trump on Monday doubled down, posting a photo of North Korea’s leader speaking on a phone. The caption read: “HEY DONALD ... WE COOL, RIGHT?”
Retired U.S. Ambassador Robert Wood, who served under Republican and Democratic presidents, said the joint military exercises are critical to deterring North Korea, which has shunned any talks with the U.S. over its nuclear program and has accelerated weapons testing.
“We also don’t want South Korea to draw the conclusion that a nuclear weapons capability is the only guarantee it has to ensure its security,” Wood said.
Matthew Kroenig, who previously served in defense and intelligence positions in Republican and Democratic administrations, said polls show that South Koreans have increasingly supported the idea of pursuing their own nuclear weapons.
“The United States has been working really hard to try to persuade South Korea that they are protected,” said Kroenig, who is now with the Atlantic Council, a Washington think tank. Scaling back the exercises “potentially undermines that message,” he said.
Seoul tried to flatter Trump
Trump’s turnabout came even after the South Koreans worked to flatter the American president, eager to gain favor on critical issues such as trade and defense.
As soon as he sat down in the gilded Oval Office for his meeting with Trump last year, new President Lee Jae Myung praised the room’s elaborate decor. Laying it on thick, Lee affirmed Trump’s assertion that Kim would not have pursued his nuclear ambitions had Trump won a second consecutive term in 2020, while dangling the prospect of an eventual Trump Tower in North Korea.
Trump just hours earlier had appeared to show sympathy for Lee’s predecessor, Yoon Suk Yeol, who had been ousted from office after imposing martial law in December 2024.
Charles Kupchan, a senior fellow at the Council on Foreign Relations, said Trump’s scaling back of the exercises may prompt longtime allies to think more about their own security without U.S. help.
“They are hoping that the American umbrella is there for the future,” said Kupchan, who worked on the National Security Council under Democratic Presidents Bill Clinton and Barack Obama, “but they have to at least contemplate the idea that Uncle Sam won’t be there for them.”
‘It’s like he wants to burn it all down’
Kupchan said Trump is not mistaken in wanting to have South Korea, as well as the Europeans, contribute more to their defense. But, he said, the president’s unpredictable approach cuts through the solidarity that undergirds those alliances “because he ends up insulting allies.”
Fried said Trump seems unwilling to “take a win” after brow-beating NATO members and Asian allies into increasing their defense spending.
“NATO is building up, South Korea is building up, Japan is building up. Trump has a problem with taking the win,” said Fried, who is currently at the Atlantic Council. “It’s like he wants to burn it all down.”
John Herbst, a former ambassador to Ukraine under President George W. Bush, said the Korea decision shows how inconsistent the Trump administration can be in its policy pronouncements. But in general, he said, the U.S. has maintained long-term alliances.
“If these things grow in frequency and in importance, obviously we will be in the process of taking apart the alliance system, which has served us so well since the end of World War II,” said Herbst, who also is with the Atlantic Council. “But despite some statements which seem to head in that direction, we have not headed there in a consistent, strong way.”
Kupchan agreed.
While the president’s language could be taken as “we’re done with you,” Kupchan said, “the reality is that, at least as of today, Trump has left intact America’s forward bases and its core alliance relationships.”
Whether Trump’s message to South Korea will amount to a meaningful policy change or a fleeting social media post is up in the air.
“He’s an unpredictable president,” Kroenig said. “If we move on and the exercises go as planned and we never hear anything about this again, I wouldn’t be surprised.”
——
Associated Press reporters Collin Binkley, Jesse Bedayn, Lisa Mascaro and Seung Min Kim in Washington and Farnoush Amiri in New York contributed to this report.

articles.title: Russian Hypersonic Missile-Capable Frigate Spotted Near Germany Island After Going Dark
articles.body:
- Category
- World
Russian Hypersonic Missile-Capable Frigate Spotted Near Germany Island After Going Dark
Russia deployed the frigate Admiral Kasatonov off the German island of Fehmarn in the Baltic Sea last week, the second Russian warship spotted in the strategic waterway in recent weeks, according to The Telegraph on August 17.
The frigate was observed off Fehmarn, a popular tourist destination, following Kremlin threats to attack British and EU vessels, The Telegraph reported.
Shipping data reviewed by the newspaper indicated the vessel sailed with its location transponder switched off, and it was unclear whether it remained near the island by Monday afternoon.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Speaking last week during an inspection of a Russian warship, the Russian leader, Vladimir Putin, warned that Moscow would retaliate against British and EU vessels that attempted to seize Russia-linked ships.
"It's nothing but piracy and robbery," Putin declared, adding that his country would be "forced to respond in kind" wherever it judged necessary.
Fehmarn lies close to the Danish straits, the main passage linking the Baltic Sea to the North Sea and the Atlantic, and a chokepoint through which Russian ships transit toward open water.
The frigate's presence there, within reach of German, Danish, and allied surveillance, appeared to mark the latest escalation between Russia and NATO.
The deployment followed a run of Western operations against Russia's shadow fleet, the network of aging, obscurely flagged tankers Moscow uses to move sanctioned oil.
In June, Royal Marine Commandos boarded the Smyrtos off southern England during a six-hour operation, and French forces had earlier seized the Tagor in the Atlantic with support from a British military helicopter.
UK officials had by then sanctioned nearly 600 shadow-fleet vessels, describing the roughly 700-ship network as a vital lifeline that funds Russian missiles and drones.
Dmitry Medvedev, deputy chairman of Russia's Security Council, echoed the threats, asserting that Moscow had the right to strike merchant ships of enemy states suspected of carrying cargo for its adversaries.
Commissioned in 2020, the Admiral Kasatonov is a Project 22350, or Admiral Gorshkov-class, frigate and among the most modern surface combatants in the Russian navy, built for long-range strikes and anti-submarine warfare.
The 135-meter, 4,500-tonne ship carries a Ka-27 helicopter and mounts a 130mm gun, Redut surface-to-air missiles, and close-in Palash systems. Its sixteen universal vertical launch cells can accommodate Kalibr cruise missiles, Oniks anti-ship missiles, and Zircon missiles, which Russia describes as hypersonic.
The frigate is capable of carrying such weapons, but the composition of its munitions during the current voyage was not disclosed.
The frigate's appearance has sharpened concern over Russian intentions toward NATO's eastern flank.
US intelligence recently warned European governments that Moscow may be preparing hybrid operations against Poland and the Baltic states, including sabotage of critical infrastructure and possible false-flag incidents.
Discuss this article:

articles.title: CNN gets rare look at Ukraine’s empty Patriot system
articles.body:
- CNN gained rare access to a Ukrainian Patriot battery that has not fired in six weeks due to a shortage of interceptor missiles.
- Zelensky said Ukraine has access to only 1 percent of the U.S. Patriot stockpile despite needing 5 percent to survive the winter.
A Patriot air defense battery inside Ukraine has sat with empty launch tubes for weeks, its crew unable to fire because the country has nearly exhausted its stock of interceptor missiles, CNN reported after gaining rare access to the system.
CNN was the first outlet allowed to visit an operational Patriot unit on Ukrainian territory, agreeing not to disclose the system’s model or location. The battery’s chief engineer, identified only by his first name, Dmytro, for security reasons, told CNN he had not seen the launcher fire in six weeks. The first time his unit ran out of interceptors entirely was in December 2025.
“This is a really heartbreaking sight when you have equipment but you’re not able to intercept any missile,” Dmytro said. “Ballistic missiles are flying over your head and you are not able to do anything with it, and behind you, there are civilians.”
President Volodymyr Zelensky told CNN Ukraine needs 5 percent of the U.S. Patriot stockpile to survive the winter but currently has access to only 1 percent. July was the deadliest month for Ukrainian civilians since May 2022, driven by a sustained rise in Russian ballistic missile strikes.
A separate report by the Center for Strategic and International Studies estimated that U.S. stocks of Patriot PAC-3 MSE interceptors have fallen from more than 2,300 before the war between Israel and Iran began in June to roughly 800, with THAAD interceptor inventories nearly halved. Coalition forces defending against Iranian missiles used an average of 225 interceptors per day during the first four days of that conflict, according to the Foreign Policy Research Institute, against a Lockheed Martin production rate of 620 PAC-3 interceptors for all of 2025, or about 1.7 per day.
The Pentagon signed a seven-year deal with Lockheed Martin in January to raise annual PAC-3 production to 2,000 missiles by 2030.
Zelensky told CNN he has offered Raytheon and Lockheed Martin full ownership and control of any interceptor manufacturing plant the companies would permit inside Ukraine.
“It will be your company,” Zelensky recalled telling the manufacturers. “It will be our brains, our hands, our engineers. And I will do my best to build the great company… for them. Because I don’t need to sell [the interceptors] to anybody else. I need for my country.”
At the NATO summit in Ankara in June, President Trump offered Ukraine licenses to begin manufacturing Patriot interceptors domestically. Representatives from Raytheon and Lockheed Martin subsequently traveled to Kyiv to meet with Zelensky, but Trump later expressed doubts that the licensing arrangement would proceed. A White House official told CNN no decisions had been made or guarantees given on Patriot interceptor production, citing the priority of protecting U.S. technology.
“I want to get it,” Zelensky said. “I think his word is the word of president of the United States. And I hope that I will get it.”
Asked by CNN whether Ukraine could build a Patriot battery and interceptor immediately if intellectual property restrictions were set aside, Dmytro said it could not. “This is a very complex procedure, and it requires a lot of knowledge, a lot of technical information,” he said.
Ukrainian defense company Fire Point has separately been developing the FP-7.x, a lower-cost interceptor under its FREYJA air and missile defense project, intended to reduce reliance on imported PAC-3 missiles. The system has undergone controlled flight testing but has not yet demonstrated repeated ballistic missile interceptions in the way the operationally established PAC-3 has.

articles.title: Why is Russia threatening UK with ‘consequences’ over Ukraine drones?
articles.body:
Why is Russia threatening UK with ‘consequences’ over Ukraine drones?
Russia is suffering attacks inside its own territory as long-range drones strike its strategic assets.
Russia has warned the United Kingdom it could face “consequences” for supplying drones to Ukraine that have been used in long-range attacks inside Russian territory.
“London’s actions will inevitably carry consequences for which it will have to answer,” the Russian embassy in London said in a statement on Monday. “The deeper its involvement in the conflict and the greater its support for Kiev’s terrorist machinery, the higher the price it will pay.”
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3At least seven people killed in Ukrainian air attacks on Russia
- list 2 of 3Activists’ bid to sue Russia over climate change gets off to shaky start
- list 3 of 3How Russian dissidents are being punished by both Russia and Europe
“London is deliberately opting for an escalation of the Ukraine crisis, while hypocritically professing a desire for peace,” the embassy wrote on Telegram.
“In doing so, the United Kingdom is acting as an accomplice and co-perpetrator of the bloody crimes and terrorist attacks.”
Former Russian Deputy Foreign Minister Andrei Fedorov told the BBC on Tuesday that “consequences” could include the possibility of attacks. He said many military experts advising the Kremlin are convinced that NATO would not respond forcefully if Russia were to hit the UK. “Trump will not allow NATO to answer,” he said.
The threat follows reports that Ukraine has been using long-range drones to hit key Russian targets, including oil refineries and logistics facilities. Drones produced by two British companies have been used in a number of these attacks, according to the findings of an investigation by The Times newspaper in the UK.
On Monday night and into early Tuesday, the mayor of Moscow said Ukraine had launched at least 637 drones in the direction of the Russian capital, of which 197 were shot down by Russian air defences.
Britain’s Ministry of Defence has not confirmed that its drones have been used to attack Russian territory. Since the start of Russia’s war against Ukraine in 2022, Moscow has repeatedly warned London and Ukraine’s other Western allies that providing long-range weaponry would be seen as an escalation.
After Monday’s warning from the Russian embassy, however, Prime Minister Andy Burnham said the UK government would continue to support Ukraine “100 percent”.
“This is the UK doing what it has long said it would do, which is to support Ukraine 100 percent against this illegal war led by [Russian President] Vladimir Putin,” Burnham said.
“We are providing support so that Ukraine can defend itself, and that’s been the British position all the way through this conflict by previous prime ministers. It remains the case with me. We are not fair-weather friends.”
Here’s a look at why Russia has issued this warning to the UK now and whether there is a risk of a broader confrontation:
What military equipment is the UK providing to Ukraine?
In April, Britain’s Defence Ministry announced the biggest-ever drone package for Ukraine as it began deliveries of at least 120,000 drones. The package included “thousands of long-range strike drones, intelligence and reconnaissance drones, logistics drones and maritime capabilities”, the ministry said in a statement.
Then in June, London announced a 752 million pound ($996m) funding package including 150,000 drones for Ukraine by the end of 2026.
That followed a meeting between Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy and then-Prime Minister Keir Starmer in Downing Street in June 2025, at which Zelenskyy announced that the two nations would begin coproducing long-range drones.
But London’s involvement is not limited to drones. The UK was the first country to pledge modern Western battle tanks for Ukraine – Challenger 2 models – to replace Ukraine’s Soviet-era tanks. It was also the first to supply Kyiv with Storm Shadow long-range cruise missiles to hit Russian forces behind the front lines.
The UK has also funded and supplied thousands of air-defence missiles as well as antiarmour missiles, artillery systems and armoured and support vehicles and has provided training to Ukrainian soldiers.
Where have UK-made drones or components been used?
Ukraine has stepped up attacks inside Russia this year, increasingly targeting military industrial and energy facilities in a bid to slash Moscow’s oil revenues funding the war and to make citizens feel the impact of the conflict, which began in February 2022 when Russia invaded Ukraine.
Russian Ministry of Foreign Affairs spokeswoman Maria Zakharova said drones containing UK components or configurations had been used to attack targets within Russia, including the Kamensky Plant, a Russian military-industrial facility in the Rostov region.
The BBC reported that these drones were used to hit military and industrial targets, including refineries and warehouses of the Russian retail giant Wildberries, known as Russia’s Amazon.
Ukraine in recent weeks has struck multiple Wildberries warehouses, which Ukraine said are used to supply Russian military components. The company itself and the Kremlin deny the Ukrainian claims.
Last week, the company was forced to limit orders after Ukrainian drones hit a warehouse in Yekaterinburg, 2,087km (1,297 miles) from the Ukrainian border. On Tuesday, a warehouse east of Moscow belonging to Wildberries was also damaged in a drone assault.
In addition to these high-profile attacks, the physical reality of the war has increasingly shifted towards the Russian capital. On Saturday night and early Sunday, Ukraine launched one of its largest aerial assaults on Russia, launching 822 drones that killed seven people. Moscow’s regional governor said the city had witnessed “one of the most massive drone attacks in recent memory”.
What could Russia mean by ‘consequences’?
Burnham made clear on Tuesday that the UK will not back down on providing military support to Ukraine.
Work and pensions minister Lilian Greenwood said the UK would continue to “stand shoulder to shoulder with Ukraine” despite the warning from Moscow.
“The Russians should be clear that our resolve remains completely steadfast in backing our friends in Ukraine and providing them with the equipment that they need,” she told Sky News.
Russia’s embassy in the UK did not elaborate on what kind of “consequences” London might face.
Russia could opt to target British military or intelligence interests overseas or step up cyberattacks and other forms of hybrid warfare. The European Union and the UK announced coordinated sanctions against Russia last month after reports of digital sabotage across Europe.
But Russia’s threat also raises the question about whether Putin would be willing to attack Britain and risk NATO intervention.
Fedorov told the BBC on Tuesday that Moscow may “interpret that the UK is part of the war”. “Russia has the right to strike the country which is supporting Ukraine,” he told Radio 4’s flagship Today programme.
“Nothing can be excluded, from my personal point of view,” Fedorov said. “There are a lot of people at the top in Moscow who are saying that all the enterprises that are linked to Ukraine could be struck by Russia because they are legal targets.”
He said military experts in Moscow “are saying, ‘Don’t worry,’ that Russia can strike the UK and NATO will do nothing. Trump will not allow NATO to answer. Taking into account the current instability in NATO, it’s quite possible that NATO will do nothing, will make a statement or will use Article 4 but not Article 5.”
“Donald Trump is still the keeper of the keys in NATO,” he added.
Article 5 of the North Atlantic Treaty states that an armed attack against one NATO member shall be considered an attack against them all. Trump has been at loggerheads with the transatlantic alliance, which he has accused of not doing enough to support the US-Israel war on Iran.
NATO’s Article 4, by contrast, states that member countries will consult together whenever any member feels their territorial integrity, political independence or security is threatened but does not automatically lead to military action.

articles.title: South Korea president stresses US alliance as many baffled by Trump order to cut exercises
articles.body:
South Korea president stresses US alliance as many baffled by Trump order to cut exercises
SEOUL, South Korea (AP) — South Korea’s president said Tuesday a solid alliance with the United States underpins national security, after U.S. President Donald Trump’s abrupt order to “substantially reduce” joint military exercises left many many South Koreans baffled and concerned.
Trump made the surprise announcement in a social media post just before U.S. and South Korean soldiers began Monday’s annual Ulchi Freedom Shield exercises, which are largely designed to sharpen readiness against North Korean threats.
Trump cited what he said was a good relationship with North Korean leader Kim Jong Un and South Korea’s refusal to join the U.S. war against Iran.
Trump’s move was apparently taken without consultations with South Korea and meant to reach out to Kim, deepening concerns about the reliability of the U.S.-South Korean alliance forged in the turmoil of the 1950-53 Korean War.
A weakening of the U.S. defense commitment could shake South Korea’s national security as it has no nuclear weapons and is under the U.S. “nuclear umbrella” protection, which guarantees a devastating American response in the event of an attack on its ally by nuclear-armed North Korea. The U.S. has about 28,500 troops in South Korea.
Confidence in the U.S. has already eroded among many South Koreans because of Trump’s tariff war and last year’s immigration raid in the U.S. state of Georgia that led to the detention of hundreds of South Korean workers.
Trump’s announcement “reveals the stark reality of a faltering Korea-U.S. alliance, fueling public anxiety,” South Korea’s Hankook Ilbo newspaper said in an editorial Tuesday. “It’s absurd that the U.S. appears to treat North Korea more respectfully than its ally South Korea.”
South Korean leader calls for solid US alliance
In a regular Cabinet meeting, South Korean President Lee Jae Myung stressed the importance of a firm military alliance with the U.S., saying that “national security will be further strengthened when the alliance is solid.”
“When we build up our strengths, our value and importance as an ally will further grow,” said Lee, a liberal who has called for a stronger, self-reliant defense posture.
It was unclear which parts of the 11-day South Korea-U.S. exercises were being downsized. The South Korean and U.S. militaries earlier said their drills this year would be similar in scale to previous years and incorporate lessons from recent conflicts such as North Korea’s battlefield experiences on the Russia-Ukraine front. They also said the drills are defensive in nature.
North Korea’s Foreign Ministry accused South Korea and the U.S. of plotting more provocative drills this year and vowed to respond with “a new level of a deterrent.”
Prospects unclear for reengagement between Trump and Kim
Kim has shunned any talks with the U.S. and South Korea since his earlier high-profile diplomacy with Trump fell apart in 2019.
Experts say Kim won’t likely embrace Trump’s overture and return to talks anytime soon unless he is promised bigger U.S. concessions. Kim has boosted his military and diplomatic credentials in recent years by enlarging his nuclear arsenal and aligning with Russia over its war against Ukraine.
Lee’s presidential office on Monday expressed hopes that a “friendly relationship” between Trump and Kim would lead to “meaningful dialogue” between their countries to promote peace on the Korean Peninsula. That invited a backlash from conservatives, who criticized Lee’s government for allegedly prioritizing resumption of Kim-Trump diplomacy over security concerns.
“South Korea’s security bulwark is being shaken to its very foundations,” Park Chung-kwon, a spokesperson for the main conservative opposition People Power Party, said in a statement.
Doubts about US alliance grow in South Korea
In his social media post, Trump said the military exercises with South Korea are not only costly but “send a signal that is totally inappropriate and hostile” to North Korea, which he said “has been unthreatening and respectful” during his time in the White House. Trump said he asked Lee if South Korea would join the U.S. in the “denuclearization” of Iran, “and they said, ‘No thanks!’”
Lee’s office said South Korea and the U.S. are closely discussing practical and military contributions that South Korea can make to help restore freedom of navigation in the Strait of Hormuz.
“Trump thinks of an alliance as an investment that should pay regular dividends, or a rainy-day fund he can withdraw from when another project isn’t going well,” said Leif-Eric Easley, a professor at Ewha University in Seoul.
“South Korean leaders understand that relations with the Trump administration will be a constant renegotiation linking economic and security issues. Seoul is thus cautiously responding to recent developments within that framework,” Easley said.

articles.title: Imagining Ukraine's political system after the war
articles.body:
Imagining Ukraine's political system after the war
Even if the terms of a ceasefire or peace settlement are satisfactory to most Ukrainians, the country's democracy will face its fair share of challenges.
Any projections about Ukraine's postwar politics should start with the recognition that Russia's ongoing war has taken the country into unknown territory.[1] It is possible to say that the war's scope and scale have had a social impact in Ukraine that can be compared only to that of a revolution. The war has dismantled the old social contract between the ruling elites and the people. Moreover, it has reshaped, if not redefined, the fundamentals of Ukrainian statehood. The war revealed the central role of civil society (including volunteer movements, grassroots mobilization, independent media, and influencers), exposed the strengths and weaknesses of state institutions and the legal system, and forced the Armed Forces and security services to adapt rapidly. However, to borrow Alexis de Tocqueville's phrase, no matter how profound the revolution, the new order inherits important traits and patterns of the old one.
The Long Shadow of Corruption
Populism and corruption have been formidable impediments to the economic and political development of independent Ukraine. In November 2020, the editorial board of the Financial Times opined on the constitutional and legal challenges facing President Volodymyr Zelensky in achieving his stated goal of dismantling the oligarchic state capture that had characterized Ukraine's political and economic system since independence in 1991. It expressed concerns that Zelensky, whom it called "a textbook populist," wanted to avoid an uphill struggle in tackling the roots of the problem, instead preferring quick solutions that enjoyed broad public approval.
After Zelensky was elected in 2019, he succeeded in converting his wide popular support into unprecedented control of the legislative and executive branches of government. During the first eighteen months of his presidency, terms such as "turbo regime" and "deoligarchization" reflected his almost unlimited power and the steamroller-like process he used to push new laws through parliament. He and his allies argued this was necessary to "reset" the political system and rid the country of entrenched oligarchic influence and high-level corruption.
However, it soon became apparent that members of Zelensky's entourage had taken over the existing schemes of illegal personal enrichment, even after the start of the full-scale Russian invasion in 2022. Since then, key figures of the executive have been investigated for corruption, including: the head of the Office of the President Andriy Yermak; three of his deputies (Oleg Tatarov, Rostyslav Shurma, and Kyrylo Tymoshenko); deputy prime minister Oleksii Chernyshov; former minister of defense and Secretary of the National Security and Defense Council Rustem Umerov; minister of justice and of energy Herman Halushchenko; and head of the State Property Fund of Ukraine, Dmytro Sennychenko. Some of the figures who faced charges—including Shurma, Sennychenko, and Timur Mindich, a businessman and the president's close friend—left the country days or hours before arrest warrants were issued, which infuriated the public because it showed that powerful figures could violate strict wartime border controls and had access to privileged information about investigations.
In addition, as of December 2025, fifteen members of parliament from Zelensky's Servant of the People party were being investigated for corruption, with some facing accusations of buying the votes of their colleagues. In January 2026, former prime minister Yuliya Tymoshenko, who leads a parliamentary faction that has aligned itself with Servant of the People, was caught red-handed by the National Anticorruption Bureau as she offered bribes to secure the votes of fellow members of parliament.
Already in 2023, one of the authors warned that Ukraine was backsliding in its fight against corruption and that the public would blame Zelensky and the government if the issue was not addressed. In a public opinion poll that year, 78 percent of respondents said that Zelensky was directly responsible for fighting corruption in the government and the military. Even though Ukrainians saw him as a national symbol of resistance against Russia, the implications of high-level corruption scandals were clear at the time: Unless the president took action against accused top members of his administration, perceptions of impunity risked undermining trust in him and damaging society's cohesion and will to resist the invasion.
The situation has grown worse since then. In a September 2025 poll, 71 percent of respondents—including 62 percent of those who said they trusted Zelensky—said that corruption had increased during the full-scale invasion. In an April 2026 poll, 54 percent of respondents said that corruption was a greater threat than military aggression, compared to only 39 percent who said the opposite.
These figures suggest that most Ukrainians see high-level corruption as a form of state treason and a threat to statehood. There is strong evidence that Zelensky, earlier in his presidency, was sensitive to such public attitudes; in 2023, for example, he publicly expressed a positive opinion about amending legislation to make the punishment for high-level corruption equivalent to that of state treason, which is a life sentence in most cases.
However, by 2025 popular outrage over corruption had turned against Zelensky. The clearest evidence of public anger about high-level corruption was the "cardboard Maidan" in July 2025—the wave of peaceful student protests against Zelensky's moves to curtail the powers and reduce the independence of anticorruption institutions in order to shield his allies from criminal investigation, including his longtime friend Mindich. It was a powerful reminder of the mass protests in 2004 and 2014 and showed that Ukrainians were willing to defy martial law,[2] which limits the constitutional right of peaceful assembly, in order to pressure the president on corruption.
Decentralized Resilience
Amid the invasion and malfunctioning state institutions, powerful civic activism, modern entrepreneurship, and the experience of decades of those who studied in the West went a long way toward enabling the national struggle for survival. Ukrainians' long tradition of solving problems in a decentralized manner when the central government was unwilling or unable proved critical to the country's resilience. Mayors and volunteers independently built ties with military units and used their resources to procure necessary lethal and nonlethal equipment needed on the front. Nongovernmental charity foundations like the Serhiy Prytula Foundation, the Come Back Alive Foundation, and the Sternenko Community led the way in providing millions of strike and reconnaissance drones, interceptor drones, electronic warfare systems, and access to commercial satellite imagery. These grassroots initiatives more than supplemented the state's resource-constrained and bureaucratically burdened efforts.
Moreover, the agility and adaptability of the defense forces were key factors that allowed Ukraine to survive in the initial phases of the full-scale war. This was the result of decentralized and self-organized networks of cooperation across broader sections of society. Just like community leaders and civic volunteers, the Army and National Guard brigades that turned out to be the most effective did not wait for plans to be introduced from the top. Rather, they independently established their own unmanned systems units, supply chains, research and development laboratories, medical infrastructure, training programs, and public-relations infrastructure.
These innovative practices reflect profound long-term shifts in the attitudes of Ukrainians, who have developed new expectations toward private initiative and state intervention, and have grown even more skeptical of relying on welfare provided by the government. This portends major shifts in postwar politics. Ukrainians will almost certainly continue to trust decentralized but well-connected networks of professionals at the national and regional levels more than they trust central government institutions or legacy political parties. Officers, volunteers, and entrepreneurs who made a difference during the war will have strong credentials for postwar leadership roles. Intense clashes are likely to emerge between wartime leaders and political figures viewed as products of the corrupt "old system." The victors in this competition will be those capable of mass mobilization through appeals to national security and justice, and who can build efficient nationwide political machines.
Zelensky's decision in mid-July to fire Mykhailo Fedorov, the tech-savvy minister of defense who is well-connected with top Western defense companies, illustrates this "clash of generations" in Ukrainian politics and governance. In his farewell statement, Fedorov outlined what he sees as major deficiencies in the "old way" of running the army and country during wartime. If Zelensky does not find a way to mend fences, Fedorov's dismissal might prove to be a watershed moment for old and new elites to consolidate and prepare for a postwar power struggle.
Moderates Versus Radicals
After the war, Ukraine will face the dual challenge of rebuilding while deterring new threats from Russia. The role of the state in recovery and development will grow significantly. This will require strengthening independent oversight and institutional checks and balances. It may also raise the issue of guaranteeing the welfare of all those working in the security and defense sector.
The public will expect the state to assist and support veterans, the relatives of fallen servicemen and civilians, former prisoners of war and deportees returning from Russia, and citizens who lost their homes and property because of hostilities. Debates over the extent to which the Ukrainian state should seek to hold Russian officials accountable for war crimes (if the international community fails to do so) and punish collaborators for their misdeeds are also likely to dominate the political landscape. Inevitably, there will be a national debate about the responsibility of Zelensky and the government for decisions made—or not made—before and during the war. Ukrainians will also demand close scrutiny of the activities of those who controlled politics and the economy before the invasion. These debates are likely to divide political actors and citizens into camps of "moderates" and "radicals," depending on whether they demand symbolic or uncompromising justice on key issues, and whether they favor selective or equal approaches to different actors and social groups.
The moderates camp will probably try to shift the focus away from immediate justice toward building a stronger state that is capable of protecting Ukraine and preventing a new attack. Figures such as Fedorov and Head of the Office of the President Kyrylo Budanov, who have consistently called for national unity and looked to the future rather than focusing on the past, might emerge as leaders of this camp. Moderates will try to direct public anger against Russia while seeking to defuse internal feuds. They will call for an acceleration of reforms necessary for joining the EU—which they will argue is the ultimate prize for postwar Ukraine and future generations. This camp will support special and "black" operations inside Russia and other countries to bring war criminals and traitors to justice.
Mobilization will be another issue that will divide Ukrainians after the war. Many thousands of men paid bribes to leave the country during the war or escaped mobilization by securing, through any means, exemptions from military service. At the same time, military commissions drafted thousands of unfit men, including with physical and mental disabilities, into service. These men cannot fight, but they also cannot be released from service until the end of the war, burdening the military and inflating the number of troops.
To address Ukraine's human-resources challenges, the moderate camp will probably call for the return of Ukrainians from abroad or argue in favor of migration from Africa, Asia, or Latin America to fill labor shortages. Moreover, to decrease public tensions over mobilization, moderates will argue in favor of increasing immigration and enrolling more foreigners in the ranks of the Armed Forces. (For instance, before his dismissal Fedorov was preparing a plan to substitute up to 50 percent of assault troops with contracted foreigners.) The idea is that such measures would encourage young Ukrainians not to leave the country because of the risk of being drafted to the frontline. In addition, Budanov has spoken out against mobilizing young Ukrainians, which in his view would threaten to eliminate an "entire generation."
However, the moderates will face a serious political dilemma. It will be hard to convince millions of refugees to return without strong security guarantees and economic stability, but it will be impossible to maintain a capable army and economic development in a situation of severe deficits of human resources.
The radicals will claim that any dilution of justice will lay the groundwork for another national disaster and a new Russian invasion. Their arguments may resemble those made in the early 1990s and in 2014, when certain political actors argued that all remnants of the old regime—whether former communists or collaborators of president Viktor Yanukovych and his Party of Regions—needed to be purged.
Several public figures with significant political and social influence—in the form of large followership in social media, the permanent attention of traditional media to what they say or do, and evident political ambitions—have the potential to become leaders of the radical camp. They are Serhiy Sternenko, a prominent volunteer and vocal opponent of Zelensky since 2021; Bohdan "Tavr" Krotevych, ex–chief of staff of the Azov Brigade; and Yuriy Butusov, former editor-in-chief of the Censor.net news portal and a drone company commander in the Khartiia Brigade. All three have attacked Zelensky for what they argue were poorly conceived and implemented decisions before and after the full-scale invasion.
Moreover, the radicals will call for the prosecution of political, administrative, and military leaders whose decisions contributed to Ukraine's devastation and huge human losses. Figures in this camp have already begun to criticize what they see as reckless, politically driven decisions that have cost the lives of thousands of the country's defenders with no operational or even tactical benefit on the battlefield. They have stressed the need for independent investigations of pointless offensive operations led by the assault regiments commanded by protégés of General Oleksandr Syrskyi, whom Zelensky removed as commander-in-chief of the Armed Forces in late July in response to public protests. They have also pointed out the absence of relevant basic military training for the majority of recruits in the Army. The public reaction to a recent independent investigation that uncovered the suspicious deaths of twenty-five recruits in the 425th Assault Regiment "Skelya" shows how sensitive and explosive this issue will become after the war.
Several whistleblowers, including decorated officers like ex-battalion commander of 46th Airborne Assault Brigade Colonel Anatoliy Kozel (Kupol), Major Oleksandr Shyrshyn from the elite 47th Mechanized Brigade, and ex-commander of 58th Mechanized Brigade Colonel Dmytro Kashchenko, have at different times warned about these and other critical shortcomings among senior political and military commanders. In April 2026, Colonel Roman Chervinskyi of the Security Service publicly accused Budanov of abusing power during the war.
These developments are alarming signs that after the war radicalized veterans and civic activists are going to shape the national agenda by saying that Zelensky and the executive failed to provide justice and security during the war. They will have a strong case to make if they can draw on the vivid memories of hardship felt by ordinary soldiers and their families.
Moreover, Zelensky himself has played a part in creating moderate and radical contenders. His dismissals of General Valeriy Zaluzhny from the position of commander-in-chief of the Ukrainian Armed Forces in 2024 and Fedorov in July were reminiscent of politics under former president Leonid Kuchma (1994–2004). Kuchma prosecuted moderate deputy prime minister Yulia Tymoshenko in 2000 and fired moderate prime minister Viktor Yushchenko in 2001. Both later came together to unite opposition forces and challenge Kuchma's regime during the election cycles of 2002–2004, culminating in the Orange Revolution and end of Kuchma's rule.
New Nationalism and Grassroots Structures
Two factors will determine whether the moderates or radicals win the support of the public and the postwar competition for power.
First, to be successful, political leaders and organizations will have to show that they embrace and practice a modern, sophisticated version of Ukrainian nationalism. The war proved to most Ukrainians that the nationalist political parties and groups who consistently warned about Russian threats and subversion in the fields of popular culture, education, and the economy had a point. The mainstream political establishment is already increasingly adopting elements of nationalistic ideology in its rhetoric. For instance, Zelensky in January 2026 issued an order to establish a "national pantheon" to commemorate the heroes of the fight for independence in the twentieth century, including leaders of the Organization of Ukrainian Nationalists (OUN) and the Ukrainian Insurgent Army (UPA). In May, he announced the reburial of one of the OUN's leaders, Andriy Melnyk, and issued a decree renaming a unit of the special operations forces after the "heroes of the UPA." These decisions sparked a diplomatic crisis with Poland, which blames the OUN and UPA for Second World War atrocities against ethnic Poles. Many Ukrainians, however, see these organizations as having fought for Ukraine's independence against the Soviet Union, as well as against Nazi Germany.
At the same time, as one of the authors argued in 2022, Ukrainian nationalism has been transforming into a nonpartisan, inclusive civic ideology that is embraced by the majority. In a poll in March 2023, 65 and 47 percent of respondents, respectively, said they thought that new public figures such as Zelensky and Zaluzhny had played key roles in defending the country, demonstrating that Ukrainians see these two men as nation-building figures amid the horrors of war. In another 2023 poll, 42 percent named Zaluzhny as a symbol of Ukraine, second only to the poet Taras Shevchenko (56 percent). With 31 percent, Zelensky was ahead of the Second World War radical leader Stepan Bandera (27 percent), seventeenth-century Cossack hetman Bohdan Khmelnytsky (26 percent), and Vyacheslav Chornovil, one of the leaders of the independence movement in the late Soviet period (26 percent).
The second factor is the importance of grassroots structures. Ukrainians have come to recognize the role of local communities, civic activists, and decentralized structures—especially military units—in building national identity. Popular units and leaders within them such as the Azov Brigade (Denys Prokopenko), the 3rd Assault Brigade (Andriy Biletsky), and the Khartiia Brigade (Oleh Kozhemyako) may become umbrella organizations for political movements. (Although its early roots were in far-right ideologies, Azov has the reputation of one of the most capable fighting units and one that cares about the lives of ordinary soldiers. It attracts volunteers from different age groups and gender, ethnic, and language backgrounds. Its commanders rarely take sides in political clashes.)
In sum, individuals who demonstrated leadership during the war and achieved military, technological, administrative, diplomatic, or humanitarian success will find themselves at the forefront of political competition after the war. The most successful postwar political forces will have strong national leaders with solid wartime credentials while relying on horizontal structures that emerged during the war, including volunteer networks, veterans groups, and informal associations of local community leaders.
In Search of a Unifying Figure
Amid public concerns over corruption and lingering questions about his wartime decisions, Zelensky's window of opportunity to be a national unifying figure has probably closed. But his political networks will give him a considerable opportunity to retain influence if he leaves office. Prior to his arrest in May 2026, Yermak—until then his closest aide—had launched a project to forge a coalition of military commanders, veterans, and volunteers with the goal of creating a new political force that could contest postwar elections under Zelensky's leadership. Since Yermak's arrest, Zelensky has continued this project on his own.
Zelensky has paid more attention to his standing and reputation among the military since he sacked Yermak in November 2025. Since the beginning of this year, he has participated in eight meetings with service members from various branches of the Armed Forces, suggesting that he is investing time and effort to rebuild support among veterans as a way to maintain political influence, whether he decides to run for another term or not.
On the other hand, former commander-in-chief Zaluzhny, now the ambassador to the United Kingdom, has emerged in the public consciousness as a strong contender for the presidency even though he has not yet declared his ambitions to run for office. He is a unique figure and is trusted both by moderates, who laud him for leading and modernizing the Armed Forces, and by radicals, who believe he is too strong to be subdued or corrupted by shadowy politics. At the same time, Zaluzhny is a political novice, and his knowledge of English and understanding of the economy, in particular, are significant shortcomings. He will have to prove to Ukrainians that he has the qualities to lead the country on the international stage through a turbulent postwar future.
Someone else may still yet emerge as a unifying figure. Ukraine needs its next leader not only to focus on healing a wounded nation, defending against Russian threats, and modernizing the economy, but also to unite political forces: If the first postwar president is accepted by moderates but not trusted by radicals, there is a high risk of dangerous civil division that will undermine medium- to long-term stability.
The Tough Task Ahead
On many occasions throughout its contemporary history, Ukraine has witnessed the emergence of new faces and new political forces. However, few of them survived the test of parliamentary democracy, especially when it came to coalition-building. Many leaders focused on their personal ambitions and created weak party structures that rose and fell in parallel with their own fate. Stronger political actors have tended to concentrate, if not monopolize, power in their hands at the expense of junior partners, and in some cases they went so far as to prosecute the opposition. Moreover, external influence, especially from Russia, has repeatedly turned heated domestic political competition into an existential fight. These factors remain and will frame postwar politics. Even if the terms of a ceasefire or peace settlement are satisfactory to most Ukrainians, the country's democracy will face its fair share of challenges.
Considering how bitter internal feuds undermined Ukrainian statehood in the past, Ukraine's key power brokers—including Zelensky, Zaluzhny, Budanov, Biletsky, and Prokopenko—should reach an agreement so that free and fair elections can be held across the country and then negotiate some form of power-sharing. Since all of them have armed men and women behind them, maintaining calm and ensuring that the next electoral cycle can proceed without voter intimidation will be critical. Ukraine has already seen in 1918–1921 a period of otamanshchyna, when anarchy and bitter power struggles between rebel warlords contributed to Ukraine being subjugated by Russia under Bolshevik rule. This time, Ukrainians must find a way to avoid bringing violence into the political process. It is vital that postwar election results be accepted and that power be peacefully transferred to the winners.
Ukraine's postwar leaders will have to decide how to reconcile national priorities—especially spending on defense and social welfare—with the demands of major donors like the International Monetary Fund and the EU, including those regarding democratic rights and the rule of law. They will also need to adapt domestic policies to the permanent threat from Russia without returning to martial law and without concentrating power under the executive.
So long as Ukraine is not a member of NATO or the EU, its leaders will have to build an agile and innovative national security architecture based on defense alliances and arrangements with other democracies, not only in Europe but also in the Middle East (Israel) and the Asia-Pacific (Japan, South Korea, Taiwan, and the Philippines). Postwar Ukraine might also embark on trying to reshape its neighborhood. Ukrainians will have a hard time feeling secure with neighboring Belarus under the puppet regime of Aleksander Lukashenko and with Moldova's Transnistria region still a Russian-controlled enclave. Once the war ends, or even pauses, Ukraine's leaders are likely to address these threats, ideally in collaboration with the West but potentially unilaterally. They will need a more expansive and sophisticated view of engaging with countries in Africa, Latin America, and elsewhere. Its new leaders will need to maintain an equal focus on national defense and on securing the economic resources and trade relationships necessary to mitigate domestic demographic decline and fuel reconstruction.
These challenges will require the emerging crop of leaders to display a high degree of statesmanship. They must understand that personality-driven politics, polarization, legislative gridlock, and failure to respect the rule of law were profound mistakes that almost cost Ukraine its independence and statehood. If the country is to win the peace, it will need leaders who can break from the past once and for all.
Petro Burkovskyi, executive director of the Ilko Kucheriv Democratic Initiatives Foundation.
Olexiy Haran, is a professor at the Kyiv-Mohyla Academy.

articles.title: Drills cut by Trump are central to the US-South Korea alliance
articles.body:
Drills cut by Trump are central to the US-South Korea alliance
SEOUL, South Korea (AP) — For decades, the United States and South Korea have regularly staged military drills to prepare their soldiers to work together smoothly in the event of a crisis or conflict with North Korea.
But this year’s Ulchi Freedom Shield exercise, one of the two main drills conducted by the allies annually, could be disrupted after U.S. President Donald Trump ordered his Pentagon chief to “substantially” scale it back just before its start Monday.
He cited what he said was a good relationship with North Korean leader Kim Jong Un and South Korea’s refusal to join the U.S. war against Iran. It was unclear what parts of the 11-day exercise were being cut and to what extent, but many experts say Trump’s move threatens to hurt combined U.S.-South Korean readiness and eventually weaken their decades-long alliance.
The exercise is central to the US-South Korea alliance
The Ulchi Freedom Shield, or UFS, is a computer-simulated tabletop exercise meant to hone the allies’ ability to deal with potential regional security threats like North Korean aggression. The two countries usually hold field training exercises during the tabletop exercise period.
South Korea’s military had earlier said this year’s exercise would be similar in scale to previous years, with the participation of about 18,000 South Korean soldiers. The U.S. military said it would incorporate lessons from recent conflicts such as North Korea’s battlefield experiences on the Russia-Ukraine front. Local media reported South Korea and the U.S. had planned 14 field training exercises.
The UFS, along with a similar joint war game in the spring, is a central pillar of the U.S. -South Korea alliance, which dates back to the 1950-53 Korean War. But it’s also a long-running source of tensions with North Korea, which has denounced the exercises as a rehearsal for war and responded with provocative missile tests.
Last Friday, North Korea’s Foreign Ministry accused the U.S. and South Korea of plotting more provocative drills this year and vowed to respond with “a new level of a deterrent.” The U.S. and South Korea have said their regular drills are defensive in nature.
Field training will likely be affected by Trump’s decision
In a social media post, Trump called the exercise costly, “with much of these costs paid for by the United States of America.” During his first term, Trump complained about the cost of drills with South Korea, suspending joint exercises in 2018 to advance now-stalled nuclear negotiations with North Korea.
Gen. Xavier Brunson, commander of about 28,500 U.S. troops stationed in South Korea, visited South Korean Defense Minister Ahn Gyu-back on Tuesday for talks likely focusing on the adjustment of this year’s drills, according to media reports. South Korea’s Defense Ministry said it couldn’t confirm the report.
Yang Uk, an analyst at Seoul’s Asan Institute for Policy Studies, said the U.S. will likely participate in the tabletop exercise but cancel “some costly field training that requires large-scale movements of troops.”
Yang said that a downsizing or suspension of military drills matters because commanders of the allies change periodically. He said a one-year suspension of drills would see commanders unfamiliar with procedures of those drills taking part when they resume.
Trump’s move could strain the US-South Korea alliance
Jung Chang Wook, head of the Korea Defense Study Forum think tank in Seoul, said Trump’s step could result in the U.S. downsizing other regular drills with South Korea, posing “a big, crippling blow” to their joint operation posture.
Lee Illwoo, an expert with the Korea Defense Network, said downsizing the exercise will likely delay the planned transfer to a system in which wartime operational control would be exercised by a binational command led by a South Korean general.
Under the current system, the U.S. military would command joint forces in the event of war.
The South Korean and U.S. militaries had earlier said the exercise would be an opportunity to support preparations for the transfer. South Korean President Lee Jae Myung on Tuesday stressed the need to complete the transition during his term that ends in 2030.
Many South Koreans view the transition to South Korean leadership of the combined forces in wartime to be a matter of national sovereignty, but others worry that could weaken the alliance.

articles.title: The US-Iran MoU is dead. What killed it and what happens now?
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
The US-Iran MoU is dead. What killed it and what happens now?
The memorandum of understanding aimed at ending the war between Iran and the US expired on Monday, increasing the risk of a slide back towards open conflict and heightening uncertainty over a diplomatic settlement.
As the deadline edged closer, there was little sign of political will in either Washington or Tehran to extend the 60-day deal or return to the negotiating table.
Instead, the two sides have continued to trade threats, with US President Donald Trump threatening last week to declare the Strait of Hormuz an American territory and Iranian officials signalling readiness to return to war.
Here's what you need to know about the deal and why it failed.
What was agreed?
The interim deal was signed on 17 June by Trump and Iran's President Masoud Pezeshkian and came following weeks of high-stakes diplomacy led by Pakistan and Qatar. It kick-started a two-month period during which the two sides committed to the ambitious goal of agreeing to a comprehensive peace agreement settling the intractable dispute over Tehran's nuclear programme.
Kicking the nuclear issue to future negotiations, the MoU was a stop-gap measure that nonetheless sought to address the most immediate crises by imposing a region-wide ceasefire and re-opening the Strait of Hormuz.
Under the deal, both sides agreed to immediately and permanently end military operations across all fronts, including in Lebanon, and to refrain from threats or the use of force.
To resolve the crisis in the strait, the US agreed to lift its blockade on Iranian ports within 30 days in return for Iran lifting restrictions on traffic and demining the area. Tehran said it would waive all fees for 60 days while the final deal was being negotiated. Crucially, it separated the strait's future status from the US-Iran negotiations, empowering Tehran to work with Oman to decide how it would be administered after the war.
Meanwhile, the US agreed to terminate all sanctions on Iran, issue waivers for its oil exports, and unlock some of its frozen assets. It also committed to develop a plan that would see at least $300 billion invested in Iran's reconstruction and economic development.
Iran reiterated its commitment not to seek nuclear weapons and agreed to freeze all nuclear activity while negotiations for a final deal continued.
Why has it failed?
Iran and the US showed goodwill in the days after the agreement, travelling to Switzerland on 21 June for what was the highest-level meeting between Iranian and American officials in decades. The following day, the US Treasury waived sanctions on Iran's oil exports for two months.
But things began to unravel in the subsequent weeks, with the countries trading accusations of breaching the accord.
On 26 June, Trump accused Iran of a "foolish violation" after a cargo ship was attacked in the Strait. Two days later, Tehran said Washington had broken the agreement following renewed US strikes. At the heart of the disagreement was the strait, which US officials continued to insist should be returned to its pre-war status quo. Iranian officials meanwhile bristled as Trump resumed his incendiary rhetoric, which they said violated the deal.
Officials from both countries soon declared the death of the MoU, and by the middle of July the ceasefire had all but collapsed. For two weeks, the US bombarded southern Iran while Tehran resumed heavy strikes across the Gulf.
Since a fragile peace was restored at the end of the month, there have been few signs that the warring countries are prepared to return to the negotiating table. Instead, both countries have returned to sabre-rattling and contesting control of the strait. Meanwhile, there has been no movement on US sanctions or Iran's frozen assets, while the American military has reimposed its blockade.
"The expiration of the MoU is, in one sense, the formal recognition of a reality that had already emerged," Neil Quilliam, Middle East foreign policy specialist at Chatham House, told The New Arab.
Both countries had already called the deal into question and accused one another of breaking its terms. "In that respect, the end of the MoU confirms the death of a framework that was already struggling to survive," he said.
What happens now?
The wider significance of its expiry lies in what happens next.
"If no alternative framework emerges, both sides will have greater freedom to pursue coercive measures, including military pressure, without the constraints, however weak, imposed by the agreement," Quilliam said. "This increases uncertainty and the risk of miscalculation."
Rather than threatening a military attack, Trump officials have instead signalled a return to economic pressure, with Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent vowing to impose measures that "have never been seen in the history of economic isolation".
The American military's ability to continue defending against Iranian attacks has been called into question in recent weeks following reports of a severe depletion of missile interceptors. It has also been said to have used "virtually all" of its precision long-range missiles.
Iran meanwhile has vowed to resume the war if the US does not agree to its demands. An Iranian official threatened on Monday to go "fully offensive" and escalate in the Gulf in a bid to break the US blockade.
Quilliam said the most likely outcome is a prolonged period of on-off confrontation. Neither side will likely risk a major regional war, but the profound lack of trust will continue to impede meaningful negotiations.
"Barring a major provocation, both Washington and Tehran appear more likely to manage tensions than seek a direct military showdown," he said.
"The danger is that prolonged instability creates repeated opportunities for miscalculation, making the conflict harder to contain over time."

articles.title: Russia warns UK of ‘consequences’ over reports Ukraine using British drones in attacks
articles.body:
Andy Burnham says the UK will continue to “support Ukraine 100%” after Russia threatened consequences after strikes by British-made drones.
The Russian embassy to the UK said on Monday that Britain had been deliberately escalating the Ukraine conflict and the deeper its involvement, “the higher the price it will pay”.
Burnham, asked during a visit to Wolverhampton on Tuesday for his response to Moscow’s threat, said: “This is the UK doing what it has long said it would do, which is to support Ukraine 100% against this illegal war led by Vladimir Putin.
“We are providing support so that Ukraine can defend itself, and that’s been the British position all the way through this conflict by previous prime ministers. It remains the case with me. We are not fair-weather friends. We will be there in Ukraine’s hour of need, and that won’t change.”
The use of the drones made by UK companies is part of Ukraine’s “deep strike” campaign. However, it is not the first time Ukraine has deployed British-made equipment in Russia, having long used Storm Shadow missiles.
Kyiv has stepped up its attacks this year, with long-range missiles and swarms of drones increasingly targeting Russia’s military industries and energy facilities.
It has also hit large depots of Russia’s largest online retailer, Wildberries, burning merchandise worth billions of pounds and bringing the war home to the Russian public more than four years into Moscow’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
Russia’s embassy to the UK said on Monday that the reports confirmed that “London is deliberately opting for an escalation of the Ukraine crisis”, accusing Britain of “seeking to contain Russia and inflict maximum damage on it by proxy”.
“London’s actions will inevitably carry consequences for which it will have to answer,” it said. “The deeper its involvement in the conflict and the greater its support for Kyiv’s terrorist machinery, the higher the price it will pay.”
A Ministry of Defence spokesperson said: “Britain stands shoulder to shoulder with Ukraine and we are committed to providing the equipment Ukraine needs to defend itself against Putin’s illegal invasion. Russia should be in no doubt about the resolve of this government to stand against Russian aggression, in Ukraine and against the UK and our allies.”
Ukraine’s strategy of long-range drone strikes is thought to be intended to cut Moscow’s revenue for the war and to make Russian civilians feel the impact of the invasion.
Kyiv launched three times as many such strikes in July as it did in January, according to data from Acled, an independent conflict monitor.
Repeatedly hitting deep into Russia has forced Moscow to stretch its air defences over a larger area. Russia’s defence ministry said on Saturday it had shot down 598 Ukrainian drones over 19 Russian regions as well as the Black Sea, the Azov Sea and the annexed Ukrainian peninsula of Crimea.
Officials said on Monday that Ukrainian long-range attacks on Russia killed seven people overnight, while five civilians died in Ukraine after strikes by Moscow’s forces.
Russian missile attacks on Tuesday killed 10 people and injured eight in a village in Ukraine’s north-eastern Kharkiv oblast, the regional governor said.
The strike on the village of Pechenihy damaged 10 private buildings, a cafe, a post office, a shop and at least seven cars, Oleh Syniehubov said on Telegram.
A rapid development of largely homegrown technologies, including the Flamingo cruise missile and the FP-1 long-range fixed-wing drone from Fire Point, have allowed Ukraine to bomb warehouses, oil refineries, ports and military facilities up to 1,500 miles (2,400km) from its border.
Ukraine can now almost match the deep-strike capability Russia has had since the beginning of the war using large drones and cruise missiles, though it does not possess the high-speed ballistic missiles Moscow frequently uses.
At the same time, both sides’ air defences are stretched to the point of near exhaustion, leading to an increase in civilian casualties and worries that the impact of the conflict beyond the immediate frontlines will only increase into the winter.

articles.title: Türkiye May Have to Blow Up Its Russian S-400s to Unlock F-35 Deal
articles.body:
- Category
- World
Türkiye May Have to Blow Up Its Russian S-400s to Unlock F-35 Deal
Türkiye’s effort to sell its Russian-made S-400 air defense systems to the United Arab Emirates has stalled, potentially leaving Ankara with a far more drastic option if it wants to regain access to US F-35 stealth fighters: destroying the systems altogether, Semafor reported on August 13.
The S-400s remain the central obstacle blocking Turkey’s return to the F-35 program. US senators have insisted that Ankara fully dispose of the Russian systems before approving the sale of the fifth-generation fighters.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
If Türkiye cannot sell the S-400s to the UAE and Washington refuses to accept Ankara’s previous proposal to simply deactivate them, physically destroying the systems could emerge as another way out of the impasse.
“There are several options for resolving this problem, and I think the Turks want to resolve it,” a US official told Semafor.
Talks between Ankara and Abu Dhabi first became public more than a month ago, when Türkiye reportedly sought Russia’s permission to resell the systems. But people familiar with the negotiations told Semafor that the discussions now appear to have stalled.
The precise reason remains unclear, although one complication may be the UAE’s own ambition to acquire F-35 fighters. Taking possession of Russian S-400 systems could potentially expose Abu Dhabi to the same political and security concerns that have blocked Türkiye from acquiring the jets.
“Any country that acquires the S-400 and deploys that system will face the same concerns, problems, and restrictions that the Turks faced,” Democratic Sen. Chris Coons said.
Republican Sen. Rick Scott was equally clear, telling Semafor that Türkiye will not receive F-35s as long as it retains the Russian air defense systems. Scott, who said he speaks frequently with the Trump administration, added that he had “heard nothing” about what the administration might do next.
The stalemate complicates expectations raised after Donald Trump traveled to Ankara for a NATO summit in early July. Trump indicated that he would allow Türkiye to purchase F-35s from the United States and promised to lift sanctions imposed over Ankara’s acquisition of the Russian S-400s.
Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan told Al Jazeera over the weekend: “We expect Trump to fulfill the promise he made regarding the F-35 fighter jets.”
But key lawmakers in Washington remain unconvinced that Türkiye has done enough.
“At this point, they have not gotten rid of the S-400, so it is at an impasse,” Senate Foreign Relations Committee Chairman Jim Risch told Semafor.
Earlier, reports emerged that Ukraine was set to acquire 12 M270 multiple-launch rocket systems from Türkiye together with 70 M39 ATACMS ballistic missiles, more than 2,500 cluster rockets, and tens of thousands of 203-mm artillery shells under a proposed transfer of US-made weapons from Turkish stocks.
Discuss this article:

articles.title: Trump says US will not extend MoU with Iran
articles.body:
US President Donald Trump says the United States will not extend the memorandum of understanding with Iran, which expired on Monday, and that Tehran should "put up the white flag of surrender"
Iranian Foreign Ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baghaei says "gross" US violations have rendered the MoU's 60-day deadline "entirely moot". Moreover, Iranian officials say they will adopt a more offence strategy with the US
Israeli attacks continue on south Lebanon, Gaza, and the occupied West Bank
And so we continue our live coverage...
