Lebanon army chief meets US delegation amid Israeli attacks
Lebanese Armed Forces Commander General Rodolph Haykal met former US ambassador Edward Gabriel, president of the American Task Force on Lebanon (ATFL), in Yarzeh.
The two discussed the latest developments in Lebanon and the wider region, as well as the Lebanese army's responsibilities and the challenges it faces. Members of the ATFL board also attended the meeting.
Haykal said the army would continue carrying out its duties under the framework agreement within its available capabilities, despite continued Israeli attacks and violations of the understandings.
Trump posts map claiming Strait of Hormuz as US territory
Trump has revived his threat to claim the Strait of Hormuz for the United States, posting a map on Truth Social labelling the strategic waterway "NEW U.S. Territory".
The US president later claimed the strait was "open and operational" and under US control, while saying there were no talks with Iran currently underway or scheduled.
Tehran, however, says it will not reopen the strait until Washington lifts its blockade and oil sanctions, releases frozen Iranian assets and ends military threats.
US President Donald Trump on Tuesday said there were no conversations taking place with Iran, and none were scheduled, adding that the naval blockade of the Strait of Hormuz remained in full force and effect.
He made the comments in a Truth Social post.
US President Donald Trump. [Getty]
Turkey speaks with Qatar and Syria on developments
The Turkish Foreign Ministry said, on Tuesday, that Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan discussed with the Prime Minister and Foreign Minister of Qatar, Sheikh Mohammed bin Abdul Rahman Al Thani, and the Syrian Foreign Minister, Asaad Al-Shaibani, the latest developments in the region.
Diplomatic sources in the Turkish Foreign Ministry reported to the media that Fidan telephoned Al Thani and discussed with him the situation in the Strait of Hormuz.
Sources added that Fidan's call with Syrian Foreign Minister reviewed the latest developments in the region, without adding details.
The phone call with Al-Shaibani also came after an Israeli air strike on the Abu Al-Duhur military airport near the Turkish border.
The US dollar rose slightly on Tuesday but remained near multi-month lows against its peers as traders reduced their bets on rate hikes, although the threat of renewed violence in the US-Israeli war on Iran left sentiment fragile.
The euro eased away from two-month highs of $1.161 touched on Monday and was last little changed at $1.157.
Sterling was at $1.352, dipping 0.1% on weak UK labour market data, just shy of the three-month peak it hit in the previous session.
Data in the past few weeks have pointed to a softer US economy, including unexpected job losses last month and mild inflation readings, leading investors to scale back expectations of a rate hike by the US Federal Reserve.
Qatari Foreign Ministry spokesman, Majed Al-Ansari, said that in April, the Qatari authorities ended the search for the two Iranian pilots who violated Qatari airspace, and the remains of one of them were handed over to the Iranian side.
Al-Ansari added that Qatar called on the Iranian side to send a technical team to review the search operations, but it did not respond to the invitation.
Al-Ansari confirmed that Iran and Qatar are in direct contact regarding the issue of the Iranian pilots, describing Iran's request for the International Committee of the Red Cross to intervene in the case as a "media stunt."
He stressed that Qatar should not be involved in Iran's internal problems, pointing out that Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araqchi spoke in some way yesterday about this issue.
US President Donald Trump posted an image on his Truth Social platform showing a map of the Strait of Hormuz, with a caption titled “New US Territory”.
The US special presidential envoy for Syria and Iraq said on Tuesday that Israeli airstrikes on the Abu al-Duhur military airbase in northwestern Syria constitute an "unnecessary escalation" that does not advance regional stability.
In a statement on X, Ambassador Tom Barrack said the United States was deeply concerned concerned by the attacks, and added that Washington was encouraging all parties to prioritise "logical discourse" over further military incidents.
Qatar's foreign ministry spokesman Majed al-Ansari says during a press conference that parties mediating between Iran and the US will return to efforts to end the US-Israeli war on Iran after Iran and Oman announce a bilateral agreement on transit through the Strait of Hormuz.
An explosion at a petroleum products depot in eastern Iraqi Kurdistan injured 18 people, Kurdish media outlet Rudaw reported Tuesday, without specifying the cause.
Hirsh Salim, deputy director general of health in Sulaimaniyah governorate, told the outlet that there were no fatalities.
Iraqi security forces have detained a senior commander in the Iran-aligned Harakat al-Nujaba group, in a move that could intensify tensions between the government and armed factions resisting efforts to bring weapons under state control.
Abbas Hussein al-Yaqoubi, a senior Nujaba figure who also serves as an intelligence official within Iraq's Popular Mobilisation Forces (PMF), was detained on Monday in the southern province of Dhi Qar, according to Iraqi officials and security sources.
Security sources in Baghdad told The New Arab that a special unit linked to Iraq's Counter Terrorism Service raided a residential building about 360 kilometres south of Baghdad and detained Yaqoubi.
A selloff in US government bonds picked up pace on Tuesday, sending the 30-year Treasury yield to a near two-decade high as fears of an escalation in the Iran war fuelled inflation worries and pressured stocks.
Oil prices also climbed for the third consecutive day, with Brent crude hitting its highest since late last month after the latest signals from Washington and Tehran crushed hopes of an imminent end to the conflict.
The market's reaction shows that tensions in the region remain a potent source of risk, with a renewed escalation capable of reverberating across oil, bonds, currencies and equities.
The number of Israelis returning to live in Israel has fallen sharply in recent years, while the number leaving the country for extended periods has risen, according to a new Knesset report that points to a widening migration problem.
The report, prepared by the Knesset Research and Information Centre and cited by the Israeli newspaper Maariv, found that the number of returning residents fell by 53%, from around 8,000 in 2020 to just 3,800 in 2024, the lowest figure recorded in recent years.
Iran's top negotiator Qalibaf said that the Strait of Hormuz will remain closed until the US meets the conditions underscored by the interim deal, according to state media.
Saudi Arabia resumes oil loadings, sales from inside Hormuz
Saudi Aramco resumed oil loading from inside the Strait of Hormuz last week and has more tankers waiting to load as the state energy giant offers spot heavy crude cargoes, according to shipping data and trade sources.
On Monday, the world's top oil exporter offered some Asian refiners Arab Medium and Arab Heavy crude cargoes for loading via ship-to-ship (STS) transfers off Fujairah in the United Arab Emirates this month.
The move came after it had halted sales for weeks following attacks on its tanker fleet in the Strait of Hormuz during an escalation of the U.S.-Iran conflict last month.
The resumption of Saudi exports could help ease tight supply of heavier grades that produce more residue fuel which can be used to refuel ships or processed further at refineries, to yield higher quality fuels such as gasoline and diesel.
The resumption of Saudi exports could help ease tight supply. [Getty]
Houthi media says group launched drones at Saudi's Jazan
Yemen's Iran-backed Houthis have targeted an oil refinery on Saudi Arabia's southern Red Sea coast, rebel media reports.
The Houthis "targeted the Aramco refinery in Jazan with a number of drones… in response to airspace violations over the governorates of Saada and Hajjah" in Yemen, Houthi news agency Saba says, citing a military source.
Israel struck Syria's Idlib: sources at defence ministry
A source at Syria's defence ministry told The New Arab that Israeli aircraft carried out the strikes at Abu al-Duhur airfield in the eastern countryside of Idlib.
Iranian parliament speaker and top negotiator, Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf, is scheduled to arrive in Baghdad on Wednesday to lead a high-level delegation for talks with Iraqi leaders on regional developments and strategic bilateral cooperation, state media reports.
Preliminary shipping data showed on Tuesday that ship transit through the Strait of Hormuz remained in the single digits yesterday, Monday, but rose slightly compared to its levels at the weekend in light of the faltering talks to end the war between the United States and Iran.
Ship tracking data issued by Kpler indicated that six ships loaded with primary goods crossed the strait yesterday, Monday, three of which left the Gulf and three headed to it, compared to a 10-day average of 11 ships.
Three ships crossed the strait on Saturday, while two ships passed on Sunday. No giant crude oil tankers or tankers carrying liquefied natural gas crossed the strait.
Some ships may pass through the strait with their transponders disabled, so they are not counted in these numbers. The data showed that the giant gas tanker "Xavia" entered the strait via the Iranian route and was not carrying any cargo. This category of tankers is usually used to transport types of liquefied petroleum gas such as propane and butane.
The data also indicated that a medium-range fuel tanker and another medium-range tanker entered the Gulf, while a medium-sized liquefied petroleum gas tanker, a “Panamax” bulk cargo ship, and a “Panamax” fuel tanker left it.

articles.title: Russia tests new submarine designed for ultra long-range nuclear torpedo
articles.body:
- The Russian Navy's Khabarovsk submarine began factory sea trials on August 17, its first time underway since construction started in 2014.
- The Project 09851 submarine is designed to carry six Poseidon nuclear-powered underwater drones and is expected to join the Pacific Fleet.
Russia’s Northern Machine-Building Enterprise sent the nuclear-powered submarine Khabarovsk to sea for factory trials on August 17, the vessel’s first time underway since construction began in 2014, according to Russian defense-monitoring channels.
The submarine, built under Project 09851 at the Sevmash shipyard in Severodvinsk, is designed to carry the Poseidon (NATO name: KANYON) nuclear-powered underwater drone system. Russia’s Rubin Central Design Bureau for Marine Engineering designed the vessel under a contract signed with the Russian Ministry of Defense on June 19, 2012. Construction formally began July 27, 2014.
Khabarovsk was floated out of its construction hall on November 1, 2025, ahead of Monday’s sea trials. The submarine’s contract had originally called for delivery to the Russian Navy in 2020, though reports have not disclosed the reason for the six-year delay.
The vessel is believed to carry six 2P39 launch tubes for the 2M39 Poseidon underwater vehicles. Russian media have described each Poseidon as roughly 66 feet (20 meters) long, about six feet (1.8 meters) in diameter and weighing around 110 tons. Analysts have assessed its range at approximately 6,200 miles (10,000 kilometers), though claims of a 100-knot top speed have not been independently confirmed.
President Vladimir Putin said Russia conducted its first test involving an activated nuclear power unit on the Poseidon on October 28, 2025, launching the weapon from a submarine.
“For the first time, we managed not only to launch it with a launch engine from a carrier submarine, but also to launch the nuclear power unit on which this device passed a certain amount of time,” Putin said.
“There is nothing like this,” Putin said of the weapon, one of six strategic systems he first revealed publicly in 2018.
That October test has not been independently verified. Some Western observers noted the presence of six unidentified vessels off Novaya Zemlya in the Kara Sea on the day Putin said the test occurred, though no confirming movement of Russian support ships or NATO surveillance assets was widely reported at the time.
Photographs of Khabarovsk’s float-out show a stern section, propulsion system and rudders nearly identical to those on Russia’s modified Borei-A class ballistic missile submarines, according to Russian defense channels.
Khabarovsk will join Russia’s Pacific Fleet once trials conclude. Russia previously delivered its first Poseidon carrier, the submarine Belgorod, to the Navy on July 8, 2022. Belgorod, built under Project 09852, was converted from an unfinished Project 949A cruise missile submarine and carries four 2P39 launch tubes rather than six. Russia has said it plans to field a total of five Poseidon-armed submarines.
Rubin’s design bureau reported plans in 2016 to begin design work on a follow-on vessel, Project 09853, believed to be a modified or serial version of the Khabarovsk design. No public reporting has confirmed that construction of a Project 09853 submarine has begun.
Russia is building a dedicated submarine base for the Project 09851 and 09852 vessels, along with their Project 20183 support ship, at Kraсheninnikov Bay on the Kamchatka Peninsula.

articles.title: Ukraine aims a drone blitz at Moscow while Russian missiles kill 10 in a Ukrainian village
articles.body:
The Moscow region is hit by a drone blitz as Russian missiles kill 10 in a Ukrainian village
KYIV, Ukraine (AP) — Ukrainian forces launched one of their biggest drone attacks on Russia since Moscow’s invasion over four years ago, firing almost 800 drones only two days after a similar salvo, officials said Tuesday.
Meanwhile, a Russian missile strike on a village in northeastern Ukraine’s Kharkiv region killed at least 10 people and wounded 17 others as the barrage demolished homes, officials said.
The countries are locked in an escalating duel of long-range aerial strikes. Fighting on the roughly 1,250-kilometer (780-mile) front line in eastern and southern Ukraine is restricted by large numbers of drones and ground robots threatening troop movements, and neither side is making significant battlefield progress, analysts say.
Putin resists pressure for peace talks
In the past year, Ukraine has devised and deployed domestically produced long-range drones for strikes deep inside Russia. Its drone technology has impressed governments and defense manufacturers around the world.
Officials in Kyiv aim to make the Russian public feel the war’s consequences and pressure Russian President Vladimir Putin into negotiating a peace settlement. Putin has so far shown no sign he intends to stop the invasion.
“Putin continues to drag out the war instead of accepting Ukraine’s realistic ceasefire proposals and ending the bloodshed,” Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha said in a post on X.
Russian air defenses overnight intercepted 791 Ukrainian drones over a number of regions, as well as annexed Crimea and the Black and the Azov seas, the Defense Ministry in Moscow said, in what was the second-largest drone attack since January 2025, according to an Associated Press tally.
More than 600 Ukrainian drones flew toward the Moscow region, where 180 were shot down, Moscow Mayor Sergei Sobyanin said without elaborating.
Officials reported no deaths or major damage. Ukraine has increasingly launched swarms of hundreds of drones to try to overwhelm Russian air defenses.
In the region that surrounds the capital, three people were wounded, Gov. Andrei Vorobyov said.
Three people were also wounded in the adjacent Ryazan region where three private houses were damaged, Gov. Pavel Malkov said.
The overnight attack started a fire at a warehouse of Wildberries, Russia’s biggest online retailer, in an industrial zone. Ukraine has repeatedly targeted the company, which it says helps supply the Russian military, an allegation Moscow denies.
Wildberries said its facility sustained “insignificant damage.”
Russian TV doesn’t report news of the attack
Coverage of the attack in state and Kremlin-backed Russian media was mostly muted, as is often the case. Russia’s main TV channels — state-run Russia 1 and Channel One — did not mention the attack at all in their morning news bulletins.
But Russian state news agency RIA Novosti featured it among the main news on its website’s homepage, describing it as “one of the most large-scale attacks on Moscow since the beginning of the summer.”
State newspaper Rossiyskaya Gazeta on its website prominently featured a roundup of what Moscow regional Gov. Andrei Vorobyov reported about the attack, describing it as “massive” in the headline. Pro-Kremlin tabloid MK featured a news brief about it on its home page.
Zelenskyy accuses Russia of a ‘brutal attack’ on civilians
A Russian missile strike on the village of Pechenihy in Ukraine’s Kharkiv region killed 10 civilians, according to preliminary information, said Oleh Syniehubov, head of the Kharkiv regional military administration.
Another 17 people were wounded, he said. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy called it “a brutal attack” that damaged 10 homes, a cafe, a post office, a store and at least seven vehicles, according to Syniehubov.
“We will definitely respond to this Russian strike,” he said on social media.
Also, three people were killed and three others were wounded over the past day in Russian attacks on Ukraine’s Sumy region, Ukraine’s National Police said.
UK vows continued Ukraine support
British Prime Minister Andy Burnham, who took office last month, said the U.K. will continue to stand by Ukraine after Russia said that Kyiv’s reported use of British drones for attacks on Russian soil would bring unidentified consequences.
“We are providing support so that Ukraine can defend itself, and that’s been the British position all the way through this conflict by previous prime ministers,” Burnham said. “It remains the case with me.”
British newspaper The Sunday Times reported that two U.K. companies made drones used by Ukraine to hit Russia.
Following the report, the Russian Embassy in the U.K. said in a statement that “London’s actions will inevitably carry consequences.”
___
Hatton reported from Lisbon, Portugal. Brian Melley in London contributed.
___
Follow the AP’s coverage of the war in Ukraine at https://apnews.com/hub/russia-ukraine

articles.title: Claims about "10 out of 11 downed Flamingo missiles" are an element of Russian information and psychological operations, not a confirmed fact – military expert
articles.body:
Claims about "10 out of 11 downed Flamingo missiles" are an element of Russian information and psychological operations, not a confirmed fact – military expert
Kyiv • UNN
Expert Anatolii Khrapchynskyi believes that the claim that 10 out of 11 Flamingo missiles were shot down is part of Russian information and psychological operations. He emphasizes, that Russian air defense is incapable of intercepting most Ukrainian FP-5s.
Claims that Russian air defenses are allegedly shooting down 10 out of 11 Ukrainian Flamingo missiles may be part of a Russian information campaign aimed at discrediting Ukrainian weapons. This opinion was expressed in an exclusive comment to UNN by defense industry expert and head of a weapons manufacturing company Anatolii Khrapchynskyi.
Enemy IPsO
In Russia, they regularly claim to have shot down Ukrainian long-range drones and missiles, while citing astronomical figures. For example, in July, the Russian Defense Ministry reported the destruction of 20 FP-5 Flamingo missiles, while in the first half of August, Russian air defenses allegedly destroyed 25 such missiles. According to the data from the aggressor country's agency, at least 57 missiles of this type had allegedly been shot down since June. The narrative that Flamingos allegedly fail to reach their targets is periodically picked up by Ukrainian activists, and recently an American military journalist joined their ranks.
Some media outlets picked up his statement that the Russians shoot down 10 out of 11 Flamingos, despite the fact that the journalist himself writes about the inaccuracy of his calculations, since he can rely only on open-source data.
Given that Ukraine's Defense Forces do not disclose the number of weapons used in strikes on Russian territory and regularly report only specific targets hit, it is obvious that the journalist relied on reports from Russia's Defense Ministry in Russian propaganda media.
Defense industry expert and head of a weapons manufacturing company Anatolii Khrapchynskyi explained in a comment to UNN that there are currently no grounds for concluding that the Russians are capable of shooting down most Flamingo missiles.
"The Russian air defense system was developed for the threats of the previous generation and is not sufficiently adapted to modern challenges, which is why it misses a significant part of the targets. Therefore, I would refrain from categorical statements about its high effectiveness," he said.
According to the expert, such reports in the media may be part of a Russian information and psychological operation (IPsO).
"Let us recall the Gerasimov doctrine, which includes, among its functions, precisely information pressure," Khrapchynskyi reminded.
The term "Gerasimov doctrine" emerged after the publication in 2013 of an article by Valery Gerasimov, chief of the General Staff of the Russian Armed Forces, in which he pointed, among other things, to the growing role of informational, political, and economic means in warfare.
It is worth noting that Russia systematically uses information operations and disinformation as one of the instruments of waging war against Ukraine. Therefore, the dissemination of reports about the alleged near-total ineffectiveness of Ukrainian missiles may be aimed at shaping an information environment favorable to Russia, in particular to discredit Ukrainian defense technologies.
Russia in Flames
At the same time, claims about the nearly 100% effectiveness of Russian air defenses are inconsistent with the numerous successful strikes on targets in Russia. In particular, Flamingo missiles have been used repeatedly to strike a number of military and industrial targets.
For example, on June 10, the VNIIR-Progress enterprise in Cheboksary, which manufactures modules for kamikaze drones, was hit. The use of Flamingos was confirmed by the General Staff of the Armed Forces of Ukraine at the time.
Later, on June 27, Ukrainian forces attacked the Titan-Barrikady defense-industry enterprise in Volgograd with FP-5 missiles. It manufactured launchers for the Yars, Topol-M, and Sarmat systems.
On July 24, Ukraine struck the AviaTek enterprise in Russia's Kirov, which is part of Russia's aviation and defense complex. Fire Point chief designer Denys Shtilerman confirmed that the strike was carried out using Flamingo missiles.
During the night of August 15, 2026, the "Progress" Rocket and Space Center and the "Aviakor" aircraft plant were hit using FP-5. The center developed and manufactured medium-class launch vehicles, including those of the "Soyuz-2" family, as well as spacecraft for remote sensing of the Earth and scientific programs.
It is also worth taking into account that these are far from all the cases of the successful use of Ukrainian weapons against Russian facilities. However, the very fact that reports of strategic facilities being hit are appearing regularly indicates that Russia's air defense system does not ensure the absolute interception of Ukrainian "long-range sanctions." That is why categorical statements about "10 out of 11 missiles shot down" should be viewed primarily as an element of information influence, rather than as an established fact.

articles.title: Ukrainian Navy Strikes Iskander Missile Fuel Production Plant with Neptune Missiles
articles.body:
The Ukrainian Navy struck the Russian defense plant Kamensky Combine plant with Neptune cruise missiles. The facility produces solid rocket propellant, in particular for 9M723 Iskander-M ballistic missiles.
The strike was reported by the Ukrainian Navy’s press service.
The Kamensky Combine plant was struck on the night of August 16. Based on satellite imagery, at least five production buildings at the facility were damaged.
At least three of the affected buildings sustained significant damage. Judging by the massive earth berms surrounding them, which is a standard safety requirement for such facilities, explosive materials were being handled there.
Analysts from the CyberBoroshno community managed to identify some of the affected buildings. In particular, Workshop 504/2 was hit, where solid-propellant engine charges are formed using injection molding.
The strike also damaged warehouses storing raw materials for the production of solid fuel and basic explosive components, as well as the polymerization workshop – a key area where solid propellant grains undergo heat treatment and final curing.
According to analysts, the damage to these key facilities means a complete disruption of the production chain. The destruction of Building 504/2 halts the engine assembly line. Since the specialized equipment for injection molding and polymerization is highly precise and manufactured as one-off units, its restoration under sanctions could take anywhere from several months to several years.
The strike also hit the air defense systems protecting the plant. These included positions of a Pantsir-S1 SPAAGM system and multifunctional target illumination and guidance radars for S-300 and S-400 systems, where signs of fire were observed.
FSE Kamensky Combine plant is part of the Russian state-owned corporation Rostec. According to the VARTA OSINT resource, it is one of the largest chemical enterprises in southern Russia and has the status of an anchor enterprise.
The plant specializes in the production of solid rocket propellant for the Uragan, Smerch, and Tornado-S MLRSs’ rockets, ballistic and intercontinental ballistic missiles, as well as anti-aircraft guided missiles for the S-300 and S-400 systems.
As part of the production cooperation for Kh-59M2/Kh-59M2A guided air-launched missiles, the plant manufactures and supplies 9G-2145 and 9D-2145 units – a gas generator and an engine, respectively – and, together with JSC MBDB Iskra, assembles 9TK1D-00 engines for these missiles.
As part of a cooperative effort to produce the 9M723 Iskander-M ballistic missiles, the company manufactures and supplies solid-propellant charges for the 9Kh820 rocket engines. Under the collaboration on the production of the 9M727 cruise missile used by the Iskander-K operational-tactical missile system, the company manufactures and supplies propellant charges and igniters for the 9Kh837 booster engines.
The plant also manufactures artillery shells, propellants, explosives, detonators, fuzes, primers, precursors, and other ammunition components.

articles.title: Russian drone attacks on Ukraine’s Danube ports hit recent high, Romania says
articles.body:
Romania detected more than 100 drones involved in seven attacks on Ukraine’s Danube ports in recent days, interim Romanian Defense Minister Radu Miruță told Romanian channel Digi24 on 17 August 2026. He said the attacks were the most intense recorded recently and that Ukrainian forces destroyed most of the drones “a few dozen meters from Romanian airspace.”
Russia’s growing attacks on Ukraine’s Danube ports put a key export route at risk as Kyiv seeks other outlets while its Black Sea ports are under attack. They also put Ukraine's southern border region under pressure as Kyiv develops trade links with Moldova and Romania, and NATO routes more military aid through Romania.
The latest drone swarms remained over Ukraine, and officials found no indication that Romania’s threat level had risen, Miruță stated. The Romanian military nevertheless remained on alert as attacks intensified across the Danube.
Ukraine looks south for trade and military aid
With Russia hitting its ports, Ukraine is turning to Romania and Moldova to keep trade moving. Kyiv and Chișinău are discussing a rail link through Moldova to Romania’s Constanța port, though Ukraine estimates it could carry only about 10% of its grain exports.
The rail proposal comes as Russian port strikes have cut monthly agricultural exports by 20–30% and left up to 10 million tons of grain in storage without buyers, Agriculture Minister Taras Vysotskyi has said.
More than 100 drones detected near Romania in four days, NATO jets scrambled seven times
NATO said in December that a second aid hub in Romania would begin operating in January. It was designed to supplement the main center in Rzeszów, Poland, and route supplies toward Ukraine’s southern and eastern fronts.
Romania faces repeated drone incursions
Russian drones targeting Ukraine have repeatedly entered Romania as Moscow attacks Ukrainian ports across the Danube. More than 40 such incursions had been recorded by early June, Romanian Foreign Minister Oana Țoiu said.
The most serious occurred on 29 May, when a drone hit an apartment building in Galați. Two people were injured, and about 70 residents fled or were evacuated.
Vladimir Putin suggested that the aircraft might have been Ukrainian, but Romania’s forensic investigation later identified it as a Russian-built Geran-2.
Romanian forces later shot down three drones in 72 hours in July, while Miruță said Spanish pilots and Romanian troops destroyed a fourth on 16 August.
Debris from drones intercepted over Ukraine has also washed onto Romania’s coast, prompting temporary access restrictions while specialists checked for explosives.
Bucharest is buying low-altitude radars and ground interceptors through the EU’s SAFE program. Miruță said drones often fly at 70 to 150 meters, and ground systems would be cheaper to use than fighter-launched missiles.

articles.title: Waiting for zero hour: A countdown to war in Yemen?
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Waiting for zero hour: A countdown to war in Yemen?
Since early August, the Houthis, officially known as the Ansar Allah movement, have launched drone and ballistic missile attacks across several governorates under the control of Yemen's internationally recognised government, which is backed by Saudi Arabia.
The deadly attacks have heavily targeted the city of Mocha in the Taiz governorate and Marib in the eastern part of the country, and fighting has broken out in border areas between the Houthis and Yemen's government forces.
Dozens of people have been killed or injured as a result of this escalation, which first reignited in mid-July when Yemeni government forces bombed the runway of Houthi-controlled Sanaa airport after an Iranian aircraft landed, violating an agreement between Yemen's warring parties which had kept the civil war relatively dormant since 2022.
Since then, the Houthis have systematically targeted Saudi-linked ships in the Red Sea, while also expanding their attacks to Yemeni infrastructure.
Last week, the group fired missiles at a Yemeni-owned ship near Mocha, killing four crew members. Attacks on the Red Sea port city have left at least 16 dead and 22 injured in August alone, according to the port’s manager.
The Yemeni government has responded to these attacks with retaliatory strikes of its own, according to military spokesperson Colonel Majed Al-Nuzaili.
On Sunday, he announced that the Yemeni Armed Forces had carried out over 180 military operations targeting Houthi weapon depots and military equipment. According to military sources cited in the Yemeni media, over 200 Houthi fighters were killed in 48 hours, most in the southwestern Taiz province.
In response, the Houthis reportedly freed over 850 prisoners in Saada, Hajjah, and Sanaa in exchange for joining their ranks in combat.
In addition to domestic attacks, the group has also targeted Saudi Arabia’s Aramco refinery in Jazan, attacking the Red Sea facility with drones for the second time on Thursday.
Political analysts told The New Arab that the Houthis are launching offensives in government-held territories to pressure both the internationally recognised government and Saudi Arabia into granting key political concessions.
These include resuming public sector salary payments and fully lifting restrictions on Sanaa Airport.
However, for the Presidential Leadership Council (PLC), the executive body of Yemen's internationally recognised government, any large-scale response is riddled with complex strategic considerations.
An inevitable return to war?
Professor Abdulsattar Al-Shamiri, a Yemeni political analyst and CEO of Johood Centre for Studies and Research, told The New Arab that the Houthis are applying intense pressure at a time in which the government is refraining from engaging in a full-scale confrontation “out of caution”.
"They must consider that a new open battle could prove far more destructive to infrastructure and civilians than the earlier rounds in 2015 and 2016,” he said.
During both those periods of fighting, an estimated 30,000 people were killed, with millions of Yemenis left in poverty.
The caution of government forces, however, could wane if the conflict between the US and Iran de-escalates.
Professor Islam Al Mansi, an Egyptian political analyst based in Cairo, termed the PLC's calculations as “protective”, with a desire to avoid dragging Yemen back to all-out civil war or reviving a devastating cycle of internal conflict.
“The Houthis are unconcerned with such calculations because they act on external orders and execute a foreign Iranian agenda, completely detached from these considerations,” Al Mansi told The New Arab.
Furthering that point, Professor Mansour Al Mantaser, a Yemeni political analyst and former professor at Sanaa University, argued that the PLC's current stalling of a decisive military confrontation is linked to the Houthis’ role as Iran's proxy, which requires operating in ways that avoid directly dragging Tehran in.
“Iran benefits from maintaining a Houthi stronghold, and various parties use this conflict to advance their own interests without any regard for the Yemeni people,” he told The New Arab.
Asked whether a return to full-blown war is inevitable for Yemen, Al Shamiri said that “ultimately, the legitimate government will find itself forced into a comprehensive confrontation, particularly along the fronts of Hodeidah, Mocha, and Al-Barh”.
The Yemeni government has recognised that a military solution is “its only option,” Al Mansi said. Any preparations for “zero hour”, however, remain “tied to specific developments and strategic calculations”.
This caution from the PLC is connected to the government's relative lack of autonomy in its position within the broader Saudi-led coalition, describing their status quo as de facto “paralysis”.
“Even when opportunities arise, and regional or international actors need the Yemeni government to take the initiative, it unfortunately fails to seize these moments under the pretext of 'fully preparing for the battle',” Al Mantaser told The New Arab.
“True readiness, however, is impossible unless the government takes the initiative to end the Houthi coup once and for all.”
Ready to shoot
Speaking to The New Arab, fighters and military personnel on the frontlines seem to share the view that an inevitable confrontation is simmering.
A brigadier general leading government-aligned troops on the West Coast front, which encompasses parts of the Taiz and Hodeidah governorates, said that troops in the field are holding their positions while awaiting directives from their leadership on a possible offensive against the Houthis.
“The Houthis have been trying to advance on various fronts, but we have repelled all of their attempts, killing and capturing dozens of them,” he told The New Arab, speaking on condition of anonymity.
“We do not currently have orders to advance into Houthi-controlled territory, but that does not mean we won't: we will do so at the right time.”
He emphasised that government-aligned forces will dictate the timing of the "liberation," claiming that the Houthis have failed to make gains on any front. At present, they are instructed only to return fire, and in many instances, they refrain from responding altogether.
“The battle against the Houthis must be well-prepared, not an impulsive decision. The leadership is currently discussing options, and I am confident they will make the right choice,” the brigadier general said.
Last week, Sheikh Hamoud Al-Mikhlafi, head of the Popular Resistance in Taiz, posted statements on Facebook accounts linked to the movement stating that their forces were ready to advance into Houthi-held areas but were awaiting orders from the PLC.
The Popular Resistance is a collection of pro-government militias formed in 2015 in response to the Houthi takeover of Sanaa.
“Ultimately, a decisive war is inevitable, and I believe it has already begun,” Professor al Mantaser told The New Arab.
“Even if the broader Iran file is not fully resolved, this battle will continue to the end, and any postponement will not last for long."
Carolina Pedrazzi is an investigative conflict reporter specialising in the MENA region with extensive fieldwork experience. She holds a Master's degree from Columbia Journalism School and is a graduate of Sciences Po Paris and the American University of Beirut
Follow her on Instagram: @carolinapedrazzi
Edited by Charlie Hoyle

articles.title: Ship attacked during Strait of Hormuz transit and other news from the Middle East
articles.body:
Trump says US has no planned talks with Iran and other news from the Middle East
President Donald Trump on Tuesday said the U.S. has no planned talks with Iran but insisted the Strait of Hormuz remains “open and operating,” despite limited traffic and a reported strike on a ship exiting the waterway.
Trump wrote on social media that a U.S. blockade there remains “in full force and effect,” and asserted that all water mines have been removed.
The post comes after a 60-day negotiating period ended this week between the U.S. and Iran with no clear end to the war in sight.
THIS IS A BREAKING NEWS UPDATE. AP’s earlier story follows below.
A projectile hit a ship as it sailed out of the Strait of Hormuz early Tuesday, according to the British military’s UK Maritime Trade Operations center, and an Iranian official said the waterway would not be reopened until the United States meets Iran’s conditions.
There was no immediate claim of responsibility but the attack highlights the danger of attempting to transit the strait as Iran throttles shipping traffic, even as it finalizes negotiations with Oman on a plan to manage the passage that’s critical to global supplies of oil and natural gas.
Here’s a look at the latest developments Monday in the Iran war and the wider Middle East. Full coverage can be found here.
A casualty is reported after a ship is hit in the strait
An unidentified projectile damaged the ship’s engine room and “resulted in a crew casualty” off the coast of Oman, the UKMTO said, citing a report from the company’s security office.
The maritime monitoring agency did not release any details about the ship or its cargo, and it was not clear whether the crew member was killed or wounded. It said the Omani Coast Guard was assisting other crew members and authorities were investigating.
There has been growing concern about oil spilling into the Persian Gulf and other area waters from vessels damaged as they attempted to transit the strait. The UKMTO said no environmental damage had been reported in the latest attack.
Iran effectively closed the strait — through which roughly one-fifth of the world’s traded oil supplies passed before the war — after Israel and the U.S. attacked the country on Feb. 28.
The U.S. is currently blockading Iranian shipping traffic through the strait.
Iran’s parliamentary speaker and negotiator in previous talks with the U.S., Mohammad Bagher Qalibaf, reiterated Tuesday that Tehran plans to maintain its grip on shipping traffic until Washington meet Iran’s conditions.
“Until the United States fulfills its commitments under the agreement, including lifting the blockade, releasing frozen assets, lifting oil sanctions, ending threats and military operations on all fronts, and implementing the other conditions to which it committed, the Strait of Hormuz will not reopen,” he said.
With negotiations between the U.S. and Iran stalled, Iran has been holding separate talks with Oman on a plan to manage ships transiting the strait, and said Monday it was finalizing details for a joint statement.
U.S. President Donald Trump reacted angrily, reportedly telling Fox News reporter Trey Yingst in a telephone interview that the U.S. would bomb Oman if it “gets in the way.”
Following a meeting between Egyptian Foreign Minister Badr Abdelatty and Omani counterpart Badr al-Busaidi, the Egyptian Foreign Ministry said Tuesday that the Iranian-Omani deal could pave the way for Washington and Tehran to return to negotiations for a “comprehensive and permanent deal that addresses all concerns and enhances regional security and stability.”
The statement did not address Trump’s latest threat against Oman.
Iran-backed Houthis claim an attack on a Saudi oil refinery
Yemen’s Iran-backed Houthi rebels claimed they fired drones at an oil refinery in neighboring Saudi Arabia, the latest attack threatening to reignite Yemen’s civil war and open another front in the Middle East.
The attack targeted a facility run by Saudi Aramco, Saudi Arabia’s state-owned oil company, according to a report by the Houthi-run SABA news agency. There were no immediate reports of damage or comment from Saudi Arabia.
The Houthis have escalated attacks against government forces in Yemen and oil facilities in Saudi Arabia, which supports the Yemeni government, and the kingdom’s shipping in the Red Sea, an important alternative to the Strait of Hormuz.
At least 17 Yemeni civilian deaths have been reported in government-controlled areas in Yemen as a result of rebel attacks since Aug. 6, while two casualties were reported in Houthi-controlled areas in late July, the United Nations said Monday.
The attacks included a Houthi missile strike on an internally displaced persons camp in Ma’rib province and an Aug. 11 attack on a cargo ship in the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, which killed four crew members and injured several others.
Turkey urges Trump to seek a diplomatic solution to the war
Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan urged Trump in a telephone call to continue to seek a diplomatic solution to the conflict with Iran.
The call came late Monday as the 60-day negotiating period to find a peace deal between the United States and Iran was expiring, with no word of an extension and both sides seemingly as far apart as they were at the start.
“President Erdogan said it is important to make maximum use of diplomacy amid tensions between Iran and the United States,” according to a statement from the Turkish presidential communications office.
Turkey, a NATO member that borders Iran, earlier this month signed a joint defense agreement with Saudi Arabia and Pakistan, which stipulates “that any armed attack against any one of the three states shall be regarded as an attack against them all.”
Trump has praised the agreement, saying that “it shows how the Middle East is coming together, and how Countries will finally be able to defend themselves in a more meaningful way.”
Erdogan told Trump the deal reflected “a strong stance to ensure regional stability and security.”

articles.title: Russian Missile Strike Kills 10 in Kharkiv Region as Drone Barrage Hits Kyiv
articles.body:
A Russian missile strike on the village of Pechenyhy in the Kharkiv region killed 10 people and injured 18 on Tuesday, Aug. 18, according to local authorities.
Kharkiv Regional Military Administration (OVA) Head Oleh Syniehubov said the injured were receiving medical treatment.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Emergency crews were working at the scene to clear the consequences of the attack.
Later, Syniehubov clarified that the number of people injured in the attack had risen from 8 to 18.
President Volodymyr Zelensky has also reacted to the strike, writing on social media:
“This morning, the Russians brutally struck a crowded intersection in Pechenyhy, Kharkiv region, where the post office and shops are located, surrounded by residential buildings.”
He expressed his condolences to the families and friends of those killed. According to Zelensky, rescuers have already extinguished the fire, while emergency and other services continue to work at the scene. The circumstances of the attack are being investigated.
“We will definitely respond to this Russian strike. And it is no less important that partners also complement our fair kinetic responses with their steps in putting pressure on Russia and supporting Ukraine,” the president added.
Later, the OVA head published photos showing the aftermath of the strike.
“The occupiers struck the central part of the settlement with two Banderol missiles,” the report said.
Protesters Rally Outside Ukrainian Parliament as Defense Minister Vote Hangs in Balance
Syniehubov specified that the strike set a cafe and seven cars on fire across an area of about 400 square meters (4,305 square feet). The fire has since been extinguished. Ten private houses, a post office building, five shops, and 15 cars were also damaged.
“Medics are providing the wounded with the necessary assistance. The rubble from the damaged buildings is being cleared, while emergency services are patrolling the surrounding area in case anyone else needs help,” the report added.
Russian drones hit Kyiv region and Zaporizhzhia
Russian drones also attacked Kyiv region early Tuesday, damaging civilian infrastructure in the Brovary district.
As of 7:30 a.m., an office building, warehouses, and a private house had been damaged, according to local authorities. No casualties had been reported at that time.
Fires broke out at three locations in the Brovary community. Authorities said they would provide further details about the damage and consequences of the attack later.
It was later reported that the distribution center of the EVA retail chain and the EVA.UA online store were hit in the attack.
The company said the exact extent of the damage and losses would be assessed after the fire is extinguished and the facility is inspected.
“Preliminarily, the fire may have damaged both the EVA.UA online store warehouse and facilities supplying goods to the chain’s offline stores,” the company said.
As a result, some stores may temporarily experience shortages of certain goods, while some online orders may be delayed.
In Zaporizhzhia, two people were killed in a Russian drone strike late on Monday, according to Ukraine’s State Emergency Service (DSNS).
The victims were a 43-year-old man and a 41-year-old woman. The attack partially destroyed a residential building and caused a fire, which rescuers extinguished.
Russia launches 147 drones overnight
According to Ukraine’s Air Force, Russia launched 147 Shahed-type attack drones, including jet-powered variants, as well as Gerbera and Parody decoy drones, beginning at 6 p.m. on Monday, Aug. 17.
Ukraine’s Air Force said the attack was countered by fighter aircraft, anti-aircraft missile units, electronic warfare and unmanned systems units, as well as mobile fire groups.
As of 8 a.m. Tuesday, Ukrainian air defenses had shot down or suppressed 111 Russian drones across northern, southern, and eastern Ukraine.
Russian drones were recorded being hit at 19 locations, while debris from downed drones fell at three other locations.

articles.title: ‘We Won’t Be Bullied’: U.K. Responds to Russian Threat Over Ukraine Drone Support
articles.body:
The British government has responded after the Russian Embassy told London that it “will pay” for supplying drones to Ukraine. The U.K. drones were reportedly used in mainland strikes this week, for the first time since the full-scale Russia-Ukraine conflict began in 2022.
“We've stood with Ukraine throughout this time with the Russian illegal invasion. We will continue to do so, and we won't be bullied in this way,” said Lilian Greenwood, Parliamentary Under-Secretary of State for the Department for Work and Pensions, on Tuesday.
Prime Minister Andy Burnham also issued a response. “This is the U.K. doing what it has long said it would do, which is to support Ukraine 100% against this illegal war led by Vladimir Putin,” he said Tuesday, regarding the supply of drones to Kyiv.
“We are not fair-weather friends. We will be there in Ukraine's hour of need, and that won't change,” Burnham continued.
The Russian Embassy to the United Kingdom accused the British government of “deliberately opting for an escalation of the Ukraine crisis, while hypocritically professing a desire for peace” in a post on Telegram, following reports that drones manufactured in the U.K. were used against Russia.
“London’s actions will inevitably carry consequences for which it will have to answer,” said the Russian Embassy on Monday. “The deeper its involvement in the conflict, and the greater its support for Kyiv’s terrorist machinery, the higher the price it will pay.”
The Times reported Saturday that drones made by two British companies had been used as part of Ukraine’s recent aerial assaults deep within Russia’s mainland for the first time, citing Ukrainian and British defense sources.
A spokesperson for the U.K. Ministry of Defence told TIME on Tuesday: “Russia should be in no doubt about the resolve of this government to stand against Russian aggression, in Ukraine and against the U.K. and our allies,” and that it “stands shoulder to shoulder with Ukraine.”
In April, the defense ministry announced the delivery of 120,000 drones to Kyiv as part of the “biggest ever drone package for Ukraine.” Then, in June, it committed 150,000 additional drones—along with 350 air missiles—to Ukraine by the end of 2026. The support comes at a critical time for Ukraine, with Zelenskyy continuing to decry a lack of aid from Western allies.
The Ministry said that drones were “proving critical to Ukrainian counterattacks across the frontline over the past months, as well as their defense against continued Russian attacks.”
Russia has previously accused the U.K. of involvement in Ukrainian attacks
This is not the first time that Russia has accused the U.K. of directly supporting Ukrainian “terrorist attacks” since Moscow launched its full-scale invasion in February 2022.
In September 2024, Russia’s Foreign Ministry Spokesperson Maria Zakharova alleged that flight controllers for drones used in Ukrainian strikes on a fuel depot in the Rostov region were pre-programmed at two locations in the U.K.
“We regard these facts as evidence of London’s approval of the terrorist methods used by the Kyiv regime,” said Zakharova. “Britain’s actual financing and involvement in preparing attacks on the civilian infrastructure and innocent civilians in Russia makes London fully responsible.”
Beyond the supply of drones, the British government has also provided long-range Storm Shadow missiles during the conflict. These stockpiles were reportedly replenished in November, according to Bloomberg.
Ukraine’s Armed Forces have used such missiles for strikes within both Russia and Russian-occupied areas of eastern Ukraine in recent months.
Following a Ukrainian strike on Russia’s Bryansk region with the use of Storm Shadow missiles in March, the Russian Foreign Ministry said that the U.K. was complicit in the attacks and that there was blood “on the hands of the British military.”
Russia and Ukraine intensify long-range strikes
Russian authorities said that the latest round of overnight strikes saw over 600 drones launched toward Moscow between Monday evening and early Tuesday, while the city’s mayor Sergei Sobyanin said that air defenses took down 180.
In Ukraine, 10 people were killed Tuesday morning following a Russian strike on a “busy intersection” in Pechenihy, Kharkiv, according to President Volodymyr Zelenskyy. “We will definitely respond to this Russian strike,” said Zelenskyy, calling on allies to “complement our just kinetic responses with their own actions to put pressure on Russia and support Ukraine.”
Kyiv has ramped up strikes deep within Russian territory in recent months, targeting military locations, oil refineries, and notably warehouses belonging to one of the country’s largest online retailers, Wildberries.
Wildberries confirmed Tuesday that one of its logistics centers was hit in Kyiv’s overnight barrage targeting the Moscow area, and Ukraine has accused the online retailer of distributing "military and dual-use goods” through such warehouses.
In the first strike of its kind targeting Wildberries last month, Zelensky accused Russia of using the logistics facilities “to supply sanctioned components for drone production and navigation equipment.” The retailer’s founder and CEO Tatyana Kim has, alongside the Kremlin, denied the accusations.

articles.title: Russian missile attack kills 10 in Ukraine's Kharkiv region, officials say
articles.body:
Russian missile attack kills 10 in northeast Ukraine, Zelenskiy vows response
PECHENIHY, Aug 18 - A Russian missile attack killed 10 people on Tuesday in a village in Ukraine's northeastern Kharkiv region, President Volodymyr Zelenskiy said, adding that Kyiv would respond.
There was no immediate comment from Russia on the attack, which also injured at least 18 people, according to the regional governor.
"This morning the Russians launched a brutal attack on a busy intersection in Pechenihy, Kharkiv region – a location with a post office and stores, surrounded only by residential buildings," Zelenskiy said on X.
"We will definitely respond to this Russian strike," he added.
Reuters video from Pechenihy showed several covered bodies lying on the ground, burnt-out cars and damaged buildings.
Russia has intensified its air attacks on Ukraine over the summer, trying to exploit its smaller neighbour's critical shortage of interceptors to down ballistic missiles.
The United Nations said last week that civilian casualties from the war in Ukraine had risen by nearly a third month-on-month in July.
The U.N. Human Rights Monitoring Mission in Ukraine said on X it was gathering information about the attack in Pechenihy and its impact on civilians.
Ukraine has also increased its attacks on Russia, targeting oil facilities and logistics infrastructure to try to undermine Moscow's ability to wage war. On Tuesday, Moscow's mayor said Ukraine had launched 620 drones at the Russian capital and surrounding areas, in one of Kyiv's biggest air assaults on the region.
Both Russia and Ukraine deny deliberately targeting civilians in their attacks.
The strike on Pechenihy village injured at least 18 people and damaged 10 private buildings, a cafe, a post office, five stores and 15 cars, the governor of the surrounding region, Oleh Syniehubov, said on the Telegram messaging app.
According to preliminary information, Russia used two small Banderol cruise missiles in the attack, the office of Ukraine's Prosecutor General said.
A local official told public broadcaster Suspilne that the strikes had hit the central part of the village, where the cafe, post office and shops are located. REUTERS

articles.title: Iran's drone strike on Kurds may be warning over Trump administration's backchannel, analyst says
articles.body:
Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi dismissed the drone attack on the office of the Kurdistan Democratic Party leader, posting on X/Twitter on Monday that “Kurdish friends” should be aware of “false-flag ploys” aimed at “sowing discord between neighbors.”
Two drones targeted the office of Masrour Barzani, the Kurdistan Regional Government’s (KRG) prime minister, and the home of the region’s intelligence chief in northern Iraq on Monday, the KRG security agency announced.
The attack was launched from Iranian territory, it said in a statement
“Nothing justifies the reckless attack on PM Barzani’s office. Kurdish friends should be vigilant against false-flag ploys to sow discord between neighbors,” Araghchi wrote. “We protected our Kurdish friends against Saddam [Hussein] and Daesh (ISIS), and we’re thankful for the security they’ve provided on our border.”
Iranian Foreign Ministry spokesperson Esmail Baghaei doubled down on Araghchi’s statements in comments to Iranian state media on Monday, describing the attack as “highly suspicious.”
“This development is highly suspicious and requires all sides to exercise vigilance,” he told IRNA, adding that he had information indicating that Iraqi intelligence was holding groups responsible for planning and carrying out the “sinister plots.”
Security analyst accuses Iran's response of being incomplete
Security analyst Roger Macmillan said that the response by the Iranian officials was lacking.
“The Kurdistan Counter-Terrorism Service didn’t just say ‘Iran did this.’ They named the munition type, two Hadid-110 drones, and stated a launch origin inside Iranian territory,” he explained.
“That’s a forensic claim, not a political one. A false-flag narrative needs to explain how a third party sourced and launched an Iranian-designated drone type from inside Iran’s own territory. Araghchi’s statement doesn’t engage with that detail at all; it simply asserts the incident is ‘suspicious’ and pivots to blaming unnamed others.”
The attack came after a report from Axios published on Sunday claimed that the Trump administration used Iraqi Kurdistan President Nechirvan Barzani as a back channel to speak with the Islamic Revolutionary Guards Commander Ahmad Vahidi. A spokesperson later confirmed the report to Iran International.
Macmillan said that the fact that the strike came within days of the confirmation indicated that the motive behind the attack was to punish KRG and warn its leadership against making further admissions going forward.
IRGC attacks Kurdish territories, 'Post' confirms
Erbil has seen frequent attacks from Iran since the outbreak of the war. A Democratic Party of Iranian Kurdistan (PDKI) report seen by The Jerusalem Post claimed that between February 28 and August 1, the IRGC and affiliated groups were responsible for 423 attacks on five Kurdish organizations in the territory, resulting in 20 casualties. The Post has also previously spoken with Ardalan Mama, whose home was destroyed by an Iranian missile.
Since the outbreak of the war, Araghchi has frequently commented on the risk of alleged false-flag attacks. In March, he warned his Turkish counterpart of repeated false-flag operations aimed at undermining regional ties a day after NATO intercepted a ballistic missile fired from Iran over Turkey, and only weeks ago he described a drone strike on Egypt’s Damietta Port as an Israeli false-flag operation.
“Egypt is considered a friend and important partner in the region, and its security constitutes an utmost priority for us. We must all remain vigilant toward Israeli schemes and “false flag” operations that aim to undermine regional peace,” he wrote. “The threat is clear, shared, and fears Muslim solidarity.”

articles.title: Ukraine, Russia trade strikes; Wildberries site hit again
articles.body:
Ukraine, Russia trade strikes; Wildberries site hit again
August 18, 2026
Ukraine and Russia traded more attacks overnight, with the Kharkiv regional governor reporting 10 dead civilians not far from the Russian border and the Moscow mayor saying Ukraine launched some 620 drones toward the region.
This follows one of the largest Ukrainian attacks on Russia during the war over the weekend, and the UN warning that amplified Russian strikes on towns and cities in July meant that civilian deaths in the conflict rose to levels not seen since May 2022 and the earliest months of combat.
The drone attacks on the Moscow area again caused minor damage at a facility belonging to Russian online retail giant Wildberries, a frequent target for Ukrainian forces of late.
What happened in the Kharkiv missile strike?
The governor of the Kharkiv oblast, Oleh Syniehubov, on Tuesday said that the 10 people were killed and 18 more wounded in a Russian missile strike on the village of Pechenihy.
"The strike damaged 10 private houses, a cafe, a post office, a shop and at least seven cars," Syniehubov wrote on Telegram, noting that the casualty figures were preliminary.
He said emergency services were responding and dealing with the attack.
Parts of the Kharkiv region in northeastern Ukraine are occupied by Russian forces. Both Kharkiv and the Belgorod region across the border in Russia have been targeted frequently throughout the war.
Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said the attack targeted a busy intersection.
What happened as hundreds of drones approached Moscow?
Moscow's Mayor Sergei Sobyanin said on Tuesday that some 620 drones had flown towards the capital region overnight. He said that most were intercepted on approach, and another 180 were shot down over the Moscow area.
Russian state news agency TASS called it the heaviest such attack in two years. Russia's Defense Ministry said that, in total, it repelled 791 Ukrainian drones overnight across Russian territoy and the annexed Crimean Peninsula. The figures cannot be verified but indicate the intensity of Ukrainian strikes into Russian territory in recent days.
Moscow's regional governor, Andrei Vorobyov, issued more details on the damage caused by the drones shot down over the capital, giving a slightly lower figure of "over 150."
He said that three people were injured in three separate districts, including a young girl with a shrapnel wound to the hand.
Vorobyov also reported damage to several mainly residential buildings, including one house that "burned down completely in the village of Kuznetsy."
He said that a drone also struck a "Wildberries warehouse near Atlant-Park" in the city of Kolomna, which also logged damage at a retail site near a shopping center.
What did Russia say about reports of UK drones being used in strikes on its territory?
Russia's Embassy in London also turned its attention to drone attacks this week, responding critically on Monday evening to reports in newspaper The Times saying that drones supplied by the UK had been used in attacks on Russian territory.
The embassy asserted that such reports "confirm that London is deliberately opting for an escalation of the Ukraine crisis, while hypocritically professing a desire for peace."
It accused the UK of "acting as an accomplice and co-perpetrator of the bloody crimes and terrorist attacks committed by Ukrainian neo-Nazis," and said that "London's actions will inevitably carry consequences for which it will have to answer."
What did Germany's environment minister say during his visit to Kyiv?
Also on Tuesday, German Environment Minister Carsten Schneider traveled to Kyiv.
The Social Democrat (SPD) politician planned to spend several days in the country this week if circumstances allow.
"The goal of the trip is to work with our Ukrainian partners to identify, at an early stage, opportunities for a climate-friendly, resilient renewal of infrastructure and further reconstruction, including with the participation of the German business community," the Envirnoment Ministry said on Tuesday as Schneider was arriving.
The minister was accompanied by business representatives, not least from companies specializing in climate-friendly technologies.
Schneider also planned to be briefed on the situation for Ukraine's nuclear power plants, including the damage to protective dome covering the Chernobyl or Chornobyl reactor that melted down in the 1980s during the Soviet era.
"Its repair is highly complex," the ministry said.
Ukraine's main functioning nuclear power plant at Zaporizhzhia, meanwhile, has been under Russian military occupation and operational control since the first weeks of the war in 2022. Its reactors are in cold shutdown status but the plant still requires external power, cooling and maitenance. Close to the front lines, the plant and the surrounding area has fairly frequently come under fire.
Edited by: Louis Oelofse

articles.title: US Awards Raytheon $22.9 Billion Deal to Boost Tomahawk
articles.body:
The US military awarded Raytheon, an RTX unit, a $22.9 billion contract to sharply increase Tomahawk missile production as Washington seeks to replenish depleted stocks of high-tech weapons, according to Reuters.
As established on Monday, the seven-year contract will allow Raytheon to increase annual Tomahawk production from its current 60 missiles to more than 1,000.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
The agreement formalizes a framework deal signed between the US military and Raytheon in February and is part of the Trump administration’s broader effort to expand the US defense industrial base.
The US has supplied large quantities of weapons to allies while also using munitions during the Iran conflict, raising concerns over inventories of air defense and precision-guided weapons.
Acting Secretary of the Navy Hung Cao said the contract would help ensure the US military maintains sufficient missile supplies.
“We called on industry to rapidly scale up munitions output, and RTX is delivering,” Cao said in a post on X. “This landmark Tomahawk contract ensures our warfighters continue to have the lethal firepower they need.”
The sea-launched Tomahawk is a long-range precision-strike missile used by the US Navy against land targets from ships and submarines.
US pushes broader weapons production
The Raytheon contract is part of a broader effort by the Trump administration to secure multi-year agreements with major US defense contractors. The longer contracts are intended to give companies greater confidence to invest in new manufacturing facilities and equipment.
Baker Tilly to Audit Ukraine’s Defense Procurement Agency After Stormy Year of Disputes
Earlier in August, the US military also signed agreements aimed at increasing production of components for Patriot and THAAD interceptor missiles.
Previously, President Donald Trump said that major US automakers General Motors and Ford would also become involved in expanding weapons production, including Patriot air defense and Tomahawk cruise missiles.
Speaking to reporters at the White House, Trump said the companies were discussing ways to repurpose idle factory capacity for defense manufacturing.
“We are building a lot of factories across the country,” Trump said, adding that General Motors was “very interested” in the initiative and could reopen several plants.
The move follows concerns over US missile stockpiles and comes as Washington seeks to use more commercial manufacturing capacity to accelerate weapons production.

articles.title: Russians showed Moscow’s air defense up close, with a "Pantsir-S1M" on a 35-meter tower
articles.body:
Russians showed Moscow’s air defense up close, with a "Pantsir-S1M" on a 35-meter tower
Kyiv • UNN
Russians installed a «Pantsir-S1M» on a 35-meter tower to protect Moscow from drones and missiles. The system has 57E6 missiles, guns, and TKB-1055 anti-drone missiles.
In Moscow, the position of a Pantsir-S1M surface-to-air missile and gun system was shown, installed on a 35-meter tower to protect the city from Ukrainian drones and missiles. Defense Express reports this, writes UNN.
Details
The system was deployed without its standard chassis, while a crew consisting of an operator and a commander works at the top of the tower. The armament includes four 57E6 missiles, 30-mm guns, and eight small TKB-1055 anti-drone missiles.
One radar station of the system is used to detect targets, while the other is used for guidance. A thermal imaging channel may also be used. The guns are capable of operating in automatic and semiautomatic modes.
Which targets are considered the most dangerous
Representatives of the Russian air defense forces called cruise missiles the most dangerous targets, as they fly at low altitude, travel at high speed, and can appear at a short distance from the system. As a result, the crew has very little time to react.
The Russian military calls HIMARS the most difficult target, presumably referring to GMLRS rockets.
Pantsir systems are being actively deployed around Moscow at specially prepared positions, on towers, and on the roofs of buildings. They are part of the city’s multilayered air defense system.
At the same time, the Russians are using new TKB-1055 missiles to combat unmanned aerial vehicles. Their stated range is approximately 7 km, while their main advantage is said to be their lower cost compared with the system’s standard missiles. The exact scale of their deployment in the Russian armed forces is currently unknown.

articles.title: Two Russian missiles hit a post office and shops in Kharkiv Oblast, killing 10 people
articles.body:
Russia struck the center of Pechenihy, a settlement in Ukraine's Kharkiv Oblast, on the morning of 18 August, killing at least 10 people and wounding at least 18, Ukraine's State Emergency Service reported. Two missiles hit a post office and shops at a crossroads ringed by homes, setting a cafe and cars ablaze. Emergency crews recovered bodies from the rubble as rescue work continued through the day.
A strike at rush hour
Russia fired two Banderol cruise missiles into the settlement at 08:40, the Prosecutor General's Office said, opening a war-crimes investigation into the deaths. The missiles hit the central part of Pechenihy just as residents were heading to work and businesses were opening, the settlement's head, Oleksandr Husarov, said. He put the preliminary midday toll as high as 20 wounded, cautioning the figures were not final.
Oleh Syniehubov, head of the Kharkiv Oblast Military Administration, reported that the strike burned a cafe and seven cars across roughly 400 m², and damaged 10 private houses, the post office, five shops, and 15 vehicles.
The Banderol is a low-cost, jet-powered cruise missile that Russia has used against Ukrainian cities before. Built by the sanctioned firm Kronshtadt with foreign components, it reaches up to 650 km/h and carries a 114.3-kg warhead. Ukraine recently found that a new ground launcher could let Russia fire the missile in salvos and without warning.
Ukraine's response
Acting Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha said Putin "continues to drag out the war instead of accepting Ukraine's realistic ceasefire proposals." President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Russia had "brutally struck a crowded crossroads" where the post office and shops stood, ringed only by homes, and vowed a response, urging partners to add pressure on Moscow.
The same day, Russia also struck the Kharkiv Oblast city of Izium, wounding five people, among them a nine-year-old child, and damaging five private houses, Syniehubov said. Emergency services worked at the site and the wounded received care.

articles.title: Russia threatens Britain over Ukraine’s use of UK drones
articles.body:
Russia has threatened Britain with consequences after reports confirmed that Ukraine used British-made drones to strike targets inside Russia. Moscow accused London of escalating the war, while the British government said it would continue supplying Kyiv with military equipment.
Russia’s embassy in London said Britain had “deliberately” chosen escalation by providing equipment used against targets on Russian territory.
“London’s actions will inevitably carry consequences for which it will have to answer,” the embassy said. “The deeper its involvement in the conflict and the greater its support for Kyiv’s terrorist machinery, the higher the price it will pay.”
The warning followed reporting by The Sunday Times that Ukraine had used drones produced by two British companies in attacks on Russian military and industrial sites. A military source later confirmed the use of UK-made drones to the BBC.
The Sunday Times identified one system as the Nyan drone produced by Callen-Lenz, a subsidiary of defence group BAE Systems. The newspaper withheld the identity of the second manufacturer for security reasons.
According to the newspaper, the second drone has a range approaching 1,000 kilometres. The Nyan has a reported range of about 240 kilometres.
Ukraine has expanded long-range attacks against Russian oil refineries, military facilities and logistics centres. Wildberries, Russia’s largest online retailer, has also suffered strikes on its warehouses.
Ukraine says seven of the company’s 10 largest logistics centres have been disabled. The Sunday Times estimated damage linked to attacks involving British drones at more than €40 billion. The BBC cited a military source who put economic damage at more than £35 billion.
A Wildberries warehouse near Moscow was struck during another wave of attacks this week. Regional governor Andrey Vorobyov said firefighters extinguished a fire at the facility. Wildberries described the damage as minor.
Russian officials said about 620 drones headed towards the Moscow region overnight from Monday into Tuesday. Air defences intercepted more than 180.
Ukraine has also faced another series of Russian attacks. Zaporizhzhia regional governor Ivan Fedorov said two people were killed and four injured after Russia launched 1,158 strikes against 59 settlements in the region over 24 hours.
In the Kharkiv region, a Russian missile strike on Pechenihy killed 10 people and injured eight on Tuesday, regional governor Oleh Syniehubov said on Telegram.
Britain rejected Moscow’s warning.
“Britain stands shoulder to shoulder with Ukraine and we are committed to providing the equipment Ukraine needs to defend itself against Putin’s illegal invasion,” a Ministry of Defence spokesperson said.
Britain announced in June that it would provide 150,000 drones to Ukraine by the end of 2026 under a £752 million military support package.
Russia has issued repeated warnings to Britain and other countries supplying Ukraine since Moscow launched its full-scale invasion in February 2022. Russia now controls about a fifth of Ukrainian territory.

articles.title: Russia says more than 600 drones targeted Moscow region
articles.body:
Russian attacks kill 10 in Kharkiv as Ukrainian drones hit Moscow
Russian attacks reportedly killed 10 people and injured eight in Ukraine’s Kharkiv.
Ukraine launched more than 620 drones at Moscow overnight in what appeared to be its largest such attack in years, while Russian attacks killed 10 people in Ukraine’s Kharkiv region, according to Russian and Ukrainian officials.
Moscow Mayor Sergei Sobyanin said 180 of the 620 drones heading towards Moscow were “destroyed” by Russian defences over the capital region between Monday evening and 5am (02:00 GMT) on Tuesday. He said 17 more drones were shot down en route to the capital later.
