articles.title: ‘I want to hug an actual, living person’: How Meduza’s Russian readers are coping with wartime loneliness
articles.body:
‘I want to hug an actual, living person’: How Meduza’s Russian readers are coping with wartime loneliness
In August, Meduza published a piece on how the war in Ukraine has caused an epidemic of loneliness in Russia. The people we spoke to described how the invasion destroyed their ties with relatives and friends and how everyday contact with the people around them disappeared from their lives. In that article, we asked Meduza’s Russian readers to share their own stories of loneliness and isolation, as well as how they cope with it. We are publishing some of the responses.
Caution: this text contains profanity. If that isn’t something you want to read, please skip it.
Alexander
Miass, Chelyabinsk region
My circle of friends is unrecognizable now, mostly because before 2022 I didn’t really have opinions about what was happening. When the [full-scale] war started, many of the people I talked to supported it, saying that was exactly what needed to happen — kill, bomb, whatever it took. Running into those same people now, in 2026, I see exhaustion in their eyes. They clearly want to get it off their chest. They want it to stop.
The only people I discuss the war and the whole fucking mess in this country with are my sister and her husband. We see things the same way. We don’t talk about how bad things are for Ukrainians — you can’t feel sorry for everyone, you can’t sympathize with everyone, there isn’t enough strength for that. Instead we’re trying to figure out how to keep living: what to do, how to accept the rules of the game and start playing by them even when they don’t suit you, how to adapt, where to cut corners.
I feel terrible, but life has to go on. I still have goals — a wedding, a child — but they keep getting pushed back because the politics and the economics make it hard. It needs to happen anyway, because I want it so much. So I try to “hit the right notes” [adapt to what’s going on].
Young people and older ones alike — anyone who just wants to live in peace, build up the country, and not fight with anyone — have had it drilled into us that holding different views costs you your freedom. I’ve already lost my moral freedom.
Igor
Volga region
It was clear right away, in February 2022, that reality had shifted — what had been allowed no longer was.
Conversations with people often ended relationships. I stopped talking to everyone from the older generation. It was like a crack splitting a rock.
Psychology has a concept called separation from one’s parents. Mine happened on an accelerated timeline — separation from my actual parents, and from the idea, hammered into us since childhood, that “society and the state are your parents.” I realized I’d stopped counting on outside help. If I got into an accident, for instance, I no longer expected anyone to come save me. That pushed me toward defensive life planning — risk management. You start leaving the house the way a peasant heads into the forest: a hostile, dangerous place where the best strategy is to grab what you need and get back out, if you want to keep living.
Then I realized that if I kept feeling responsible for everything, playing the good Samaritan the way I used to, I’d burn out and stop functioning — there’s simply too much evil around. So I gradually grew callous. My zone of responsibility shrank to 100 square meters (1,076 square feet) and three living creatures.
News that someone died somewhere no longer gets a reaction out of me. They died. We haven’t, not yet. If I die, everyone else will be just as indifferent, and that’s fine.
I had to stop communicating in Russian online. At some point it hit me that the man at the top had privatized the language. It’s his now, not mine — he decides what can and can’t be said in it. So screw him, I thought, let him choke on it. I’ve stopped consuming almost all Russian-language content, because nothing honest can come out of a privatized language, and I’m not even going to look for it. The one exception is a short list of outlets, including Meduza, which I keep around for warnings about imminent dangers.
In the end I started talking exclusively to foreigners, on foreign platforms, in English. There you barely have to censor yourself, though you do have to stay mindful of their own sensitive topics. That’s hard. But in some ways it’s easier — compared to the police, being cancelled is nothing, and the cost of a mistake is lower.
When ChatGPT entered my life in 2025, I felt enormous relief. Finally there was something that could sustain a discussion — probably better than anyone I know — without taking offense, while helping me refine and clarify my model of the world through dialogue. Now I can do that without other people, and without risking that someone will inform on me.
I’m essentially waiting for a technological revolution that will render today’s problems irrelevant, make countries and states redundant, and genuinely expand every individual’s capabilities. I’m waiting for the day the need to communicate directly with other people disappears entirely, because we don’t know how anymore and don’t want to learn.
I, for one, definitely don’t want to anymore. I’d rather hand my thoughts to an AI agent and let it discuss everything with the equivalent agent belonging to another person or organization. Let there be a layer like that, one capable of smoothing over the rough edges. Communication should be handled by an entity without a limbic system.
A decade or two from now, we’ll all be embarrassed to remember that we were even capable of waging war and squeezing each other economically over borders and flags nobody cares about — the way we now look back on the Crusades. But knowing a little more about humanity by then, we won’t talk about it. We’ll just pretend the 2020s never happened.
I no longer accept the concept of the nation-state at all. We don’t live on Earth, or in Europe or Asia, or in some particular nation-state — we live in a city or a village. Some people never venture beyond a few courtyards their whole lives.
I don’t want to fix a broken state. We’ve already spent decades trying and haven’t succeeded. It’s like an old car — at some point it’s simpler to send it to the junkyard and replace it with something conceptually new.
Andrey
Moscow
Before the [full-scale] war I had a large circle of friends and socialized constantly. Most of my closest friends scattered to different countries once the war and the mobilization began.
I didn’t leave — I have an elderly mother, and she has no one but me. Besides, I don’t speak any foreign languages and have no idea what I’d even do abroad.
I’ve always been interested in politics and tried to stay involved for as long as it was possible. Even if I could move to another country, I’d have no way to take part in political life there, and that doesn’t exactly make me want to leave.
To keep from losing my mind, I spent a couple of years on antidepressants after the war started, and thanks to them I quit drinking entirely. I decided that if I didn’t quit, I’d drink myself to death. Not long after February 24, the war had already claimed a friend of mine who couldn’t cope psychologically, started drinking, and, because of the alcohol, failed to give himself his insulin shot in time. He died.
Now I have to economize on antidepressants. I’m a freelancer in video production, and there’s less and less work, so I can’t afford a good therapist anymore. Going to the psychiatric clinic is terrifying.
I’ve had to cut ties with a bunch of people over their views since the war started. With some relatives and colleagues I now keep contact to a minimum. Only a handful of people are left with whom I can freely discuss what’s happening in the country.
The gist of it: I’ve retreated into internal emigration, just like Brodsky. I rarely leave the house except for work meetings with clients. You walk out of your building, see a poster for United Russia, tear it down — and a week later it’s back up again.
Spending so much time alone at home, I’ve gone back to playing video games the way I did as a teenager. Neural networks help keep me from losing my mind — I use them to dig into topics like the biography of Valentin Sokolov. It’s sad that I couldn’t find a single documentary about him, and I hope to make one myself someday. I also sometimes ask AI to talk with me as if it were a psychologist. And AI sex chats fill the loneliness that comes with not having relationships with women.
Anonymous reader
Moscow
I’m generally a solitary person, but once the [full-scale] war started I felt a much sharper need to find people like myself. I read people like me on Facebook, sure, but that’s not the same — I want to hug an actual, living person.
I can’t help myself — I throw probing, often careless remarks at everyone I run into: cab drivers, workers at pickup points, people I share an elevator with. My husband complains, but I can’t resist. For me it’s a kind of homemade sociology. I really want to know what’s going on in society.
Igor
Perm
I was living in St. Petersburg when the [full-scale] war started, but moved back to Perm in 2024 for family reasons.
Things are very bad here. In St. Petersburg I’d had a small antiwar circle of friends, but that disappeared the moment I moved. Now I’m immersed in an atmosphere of total support for the war — here it’s as natural as the weather. Whether what’s happening is “right” isn’t even up for discussion. What people do discuss is the deaths of mutual acquaintances (heroic ones, of course), weapons, new drones, “the West’s cunning plans.”
Neighbors greet SVO soldiers with vodka and snacks and sing at the top of their lungs until morning. Volunteers sewing camouflage netting look for helpers, and find them. Schoolkids run around the streets teasing each other: “You’re a Ukrainian — no, you are — no, you are — Ukrainian, Ukrainian, Ukes.” War and hatred are welded into the minds of people in this region.
Finding antiwar-minded people here is simply unrealistic. I feel locked in a prison of fear. All I have left is my family, who share my views — we’ve walled ourselves off and cut contact with the outside world, relatives included.
Changing the situation is practically impossible. I can’t leave, mainly for financial reasons, and I can’t leave my parents behind either. All that’s left is to accept it and wait. Real life is over. All that’s left is its empty shell.
Anonymous reader
There’s almost no one to discuss the war with anymore. Even everyday concerns and worries have become hard to talk about the way they used to be. I feel loneliness, deep sadness, powerlessness.
I discuss it with my therapist and with my boyfriend, though he’s not fully engaged — mostly I’m just venting. I try to spend time relaxing in nature and being around animals to cope with my psychological state. I keep my hope alive, do what I have to, and take small steps toward peace.
Alexander
Moscow region
In February 2022, when it all began, I was in the middle of changing my life — I’d taken a new job in a different field and made a lot of new acquaintances. I remember thinking: “This is going to be hard now, not just because I’m an introvert but because of what’s happening. How am I supposed to get along with new people if they’re “Za”? What if my new boss turns out to be one of them?”
But, strangely enough, no. I joined a large Telegram chat for specialists in my field from all over Russia, scrolled through the pinned messages, and found that people were horrified — but there were no war supporters there, or at least none who made themselves visible. When outright “Z-patriots” do wander in, they’re quickly shown the door. Back at the start of the war, some of the pinned messages were even strikingly respectful, along the lines of: “Given the latest news, let’s support our colleagues in Ukraine.”
I’ve since run into the same thing offline. I’m a freelancer who works with a lot of people and projects, and I go to gatherings now and then — everywhere it’s the same consensus. We either don’t mention the topic at all, or we bring it up cautiously, sadly, calling it “the trouble.” At business meetings and at parties alike, no one ever talks about the war directly, but from the averted eyes and the muttering through gritted teeth, I can tell everyone finds it deeply repulsive. A few times I got bolder and spoke more directly about it in private conversations, and every time, people clearly backed me up.
I’ve realized I’m surrounded by a lot of people who have both a heart and a functioning brain — more of them than I expected. When someone who supports the war does turn up, which is rare, I try to wrap up the conversation quickly. Trying to change their mind is both pointless and dangerous.
Alexander
Volzhsky, Volgograd region
My circle of friends shrank sharply, but I put that down to moving — I lived in Moscow from 2019 to 2023, then went back to my hometown.
At the start of the war, my close friends and I discussed it constantly. Then half of them left the country, though, to be fair, almost all of them later came back. Now I only discuss the topic openly with my fiancée, and even then only at home and quietly. I’m glad she shares my views.
I like to think I’m changing the situation. I try to be kind even to aggressive people, though it doesn’t always work since I can be harsh myself. People latch onto that these days, I think, and it makes them happy. I get the sense that people are tired of violence, rudeness, militarism, and all the other crap on TV — tired of the government’s rhetoric. But at the same time, it doesn’t seem to take much these days for a person in Russia to slide into hatred, violence, and radicalism. Then again, maybe I’m just judging by myself.
Polina
Ryazan
My circle of friends hasn’t changed since the [full-scale] war started, but my husband and I have gotten very careful about how we phrase things around people who support it. We don’t bring up the topic with our closest friends — we know where they stand, and we don’t want to lose friendships that go back years.
It’s a relief that my husband and I support each other and see things the same way. Without his support it would be hard, and I’d definitely feel lonely. My mother used to support all this “hype,” but she’s gradually starting to see the truth, which makes me very happy.
I try to focus on life’s small things — good food, new clothes, pleasant moments with loved ones, short trips to nearby towns. I do a bit of volunteering, helping clear the city’s riverside embankment along with other people who care. Some part of me is looking for a way to protest safely, but I haven’t found one yet.
Veronika
Moscow
I don’t really have friends anymore. In 2022 and 2023 I talked to people about the war constantly, trying to change their minds, and at some point it stopped seeming to mean anything. Now it’s just become awkward to even bring up the topic.
I managed to change my fiancé‘s mind, but no one else’s. I went to see [Boris] Nadezhdin, to vote in the [March 2024 presidential] election, to the Solovetsky Stone, to [Alexey Navalny’s] grave. I just loved being around people like me, watching them, even in silence — glad at how different they are and how many of them there are.
At Meduza, we are committed to transparency about our use of artificial intelligence in the newsroom. The story you’re reading was written by one of our living, breathing journalists and translated from Russian using an AI model configured to follow our strict editorial standards. This translation process is the result of extensive testing and refinements to ensure our English-language coverage is timely and accurate. A Meduza editor reviews every draft before publication.
If you find any errors in this translation, please contact us at [email protected].
To read Meduza’s exclusive content in English, please subscribe to our newsletter.

articles.title: Trump threatened to bomb Oman because he’s unhappy with country’s deal with Iran, officials say
articles.body:
Trump threatened to bomb Oman because he’s unhappy with country’s deal with Iran, officials say
CAIRO (AP) — U.S. President Donald Trump threatened to bomb Oman because he is unhappy the country is close to a deal with Iran to manage ship traffic through the Strait of Hormuz, two regional officials said Tuesday, a day after Trump leveled the threat.
The officials said the Trump administration has told Oman it is opposed to parts of the yet-to-be-announced deal, including the joint Iranian and Omani management of the exit route out of the passage that’s critical to global supplies of oil and natural gas. The officials were briefed on the U.S. position and how the administration views Oman’s position.
Meanwhile, a projectile hit a ship as it sailed out of the strait, according to the British military’s maritime monitoring agency, and an Iranian official said the waterway would not reopen until the United States meets Iran’s conditions.
US believes Oman has not been tough enough with Iran
The U.S. believes Oman has not been tough enough in its negotiations with Iran and is unhappy with Oman’s agreement to collect voluntary fees from vessels, even if the charges are related to security and maritime environmental protection, according to the officials, who spoke on condition of anonymity because they were not authorized to talk to journalists.
Trump on Monday threatened to bomb Oman as it works with Iran on a deal to open the strait and pave the way for the U.S. and Iran to resume negotiations to end the war.
He posted a map on social media Tuesday depicting the strait as a U.S. territory. The president first mentioned the idea in an offhand comment last week. On Monday, he told reporters in the Oval Office, “I like the idea of declaring it a territory,” without providing details.
The White House on Tuesday referred to Trump’s remarks in the Oval Office and declined to comment further about Oman.
Iran refers to Trump’s ‘delusion’ about the strait
Iranian Deputy Foreign Minister Kazem Gharibabadi appeared to respond to Trump’s post on social media depicting the strait as American territory.
“Just as Trump correctly wrote the name of the eternal Persian Gulf, his delusion regarding the Strait of Hormuz will soon either be corrected, or we will correct this deluded man’s delusions for him,” Gharibabadi wrote on X.
Trump’s comment on Monday was not the first time he has threatened Oman. In May, he told reporters during a Cabinet meeting that Oman “will behave just like everybody else, or we will have to blow them up.”
Iran reiterated Tuesday that Tehran plans to maintain its grip on shipping traffic until Washington meets its conditions.
“Until the United States fulfills its commitments under the agreement, including lifting the blockade, releasing frozen assets, lifting oil sanctions, ending threats and military operations on all fronts, and implementing the other conditions to which it committed, the Strait of Hormuz will not reopen,” said Mohammad Bagher Qalibaf, Iran’s parliamentary speaker and negotiator in previous talks with the U.S.
The Egyptian Foreign Ministry said Tuesday that the Iranian-Omani deal could pave the way for Washington and Tehran to return to negotiations for a “comprehensive and permanent deal that addresses all concerns and enhances regional security and stability.”
The statement came after a meeting between Egyptian Foreign Minister Badr Abdelatty and Omani counterpart Badr al-Busaidi. But it did not address Trump’s latest threat against Oman.
President insists strait is open as more attacks are reported
Trump said Tuesday the U.S. has no planned talks with Iran but insisted the strait is “open and operating,” despite limited traffic, the reported boat strike and the end on Monday of the 60-day negotiating period between the countries.
Trump wrote on social media that a U.S. blockade of the strait remains “in full force and effect,” adding that all water mines have been removed.
As the talks between Iran and Oman continue, more attacks were reported in the region.
An unidentified projectile hit a ship early Tuesday in the strait off the coast of Oman, damaging the engine room and causing a casualty, according to the U.K. Maritime Trade Operations center.
The monitoring agency did not release any details about the ship or its cargo, and it was unclear whether the crew member was killed or wounded. The agency said the Omani Coast Guard was assisting other crew members and that authorities were investigating.
And Yemen’s Iran-backed Houthi rebels claimed they fired drones at an oil refinery in neighboring Saudi Arabia, the latest attack that threatened to reignite Yemen’s civil war and open another front in the Middle East.
The attack targeted a facility run by Saudi Aramco, Saudi Arabia’s state-owned oil company, according to a report by the Houthi-run SABA news agency. There were no immediate reports of damage or comment from Saudi Arabia.

articles.title: US, Canada hold last-minute talks to stop 50% U.S. tariffs on $20 billion worth of Canadian goods
articles.body:
US and Canada hold last-minute talks to stop Trump’s 50% tariffs
WASHINGTON (AP) — The U.S. and Canada are negotiating in an effort to reach a truce on tariffs before a 12:01 a.m. Wednesday deadline set by U.S. President Donald Trump.
If no deal is reached, Trump has threatened to impose 50% tariffs on $20 billion worth of Canadian products, ranging from hockey sticks to tongue depressors.
″We are negotiating,” Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney told reporters Monday, speaking in French. “The negotiations are very intense and delicate. This is not the time to talk about negotiations in public.”
Carney and Trump spoke by phone Monday afternoon about the ongoing trade negotiations, Carney’s office said, underscoring the last-minute push to reach a deal before Wednesday’s deadline.
The two countries have wrangled for decades over trade, poking each other over sore spots like Canadian softwood lumber imports and U.S. access to Canada’s protected dairy market.
Somehow they still managed to remain friends, allies and trading partners. Canadian soldiers fought alongside Americans in Afghanistan after 9/11. The 5,525-mile U.S.-Canada border is undefended, and nearly 330,000 people and $2 billion worth of goods cross it every day; 800,000 Canadians live in the United States.
Trump’s approach to dealing with Canada marks an extraordinary departure from the traditionally cooperative relationship between the two countries. Trump has hit Canadian goods with tariffs — in a push to bring manufacturing back to the United States — and has repeatedly made inflammatory comments about turning Canada into America’s 51st state.
The Canadian public is fed up. A petition to expel the U.S. ambassador, a Trump ally, has collected nearly 218,000 signatures since July 21. It accuses Ambassador Pete Hoekstra of having “normalized’’ Trump’s talk of annexing Canada, among other things.
Looking for an off-ramp
Nearly 72% of Canada’s goods exports last year went to the United States. And the Trump administration might be wary of imposing a hefty new tariff — paid by U.S. importers who try to pass along the cost to consumers via higher prices — ahead of November’s midterm elections. American voters are already frustrated with the high cost of living.
“I don’t think either side really wants these tariffs to come into effect,’’ said Ryan Majerus, a partner at King & Spalding and a former U.S. trade official. “There’s a pretty strong push on both sides to find an off ramp here.’’
Majerus said the United States is aiming to get Canada to buy more U.S. military equipment, including F-35 fighters; to take part in Trump’s “Golden Dome’’ missile defense; and to give the United States more access to critical minerals, thereby reducing America’s reliance on tenuous supplies from its geopolitical rival, China.
The Canadians would like relief from U.S. tariffs on steel and aluminum as well as softwood lumber, which America says receives unfair government subsidies.
Trump relies on Smoot-Hawley to go after Canada
Trump has made tariffs the centerpiece of his second-term economic agenda. Last year, he imposed double-digit import taxes on almost every country on earth, justifying them by declaring the longstanding U.S. trade deficit a national emergency. The Supreme Court in February ruled that he’d overstepped his authority, striking down those tariffs and setting the stage for the federal government to pay refunds to importers.
Trump immediately looked for other ways to rebuild his tariff wall. Last month, he imposed import taxes of 10% to 12.5% on 59 countries and the European Union — which together account for 99% of U.S. imports — for allegedly failing to have or to enforce restrictions on imports made from forced labor.
Then he reached back to the Great Depression to find a cudgel with which to whack Canada, one of his favorite targets.
Trump invoked Section 338 of the Tariff Act of 1930 to impose 50% tariffs on products that account for about 5% of Canadian exports to the United States.
Nearly a century ago, with the U.S. and world economies in collapse, Congress passed the 1930 tariff law, imposing hefty taxes on imports from around the world. Known as the Smoot-Hawley tariffs, named for their congressional sponsors, they are notorious among economists and historians for limiting world commerce and making the Great Depression worse.
Section 338 tariffs have never been used before. U.S. trade negotiators traditionally have favored another tool, Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974 — the provision Trump invoked to impose last month’s forced-labor tariffs.
Section 338 authorizes the president to impose tariffs of up to 50% on imports from countries that have discriminated against U.S. businesses. Unlike Section 301 sanctions, no investigation is required. Nor is there any limit on how long the tariffs can stay in place.
In announcing the Section 338 tariffs, Trump claimed that Canada discriminates against American exports of autos, alcohol and cheese. Trump is angry because Canada and China were the only countries that punched back with retaliatory tariffs of their own when he slapped levies on their products last year.
“If a country retaliates against us, we’re obviously not going to tolerate that,” U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer told reporters Friday at the Iowa State Fair. “We’ll take action. My sense is the Canadians, they want to have a more conciliatory approach, but we’ll see.”
New leverage to renegotiate USMCA
The U.S. is renegotiating a North American trade pact — the US-Mexico-Canada Agreement — that Trump strong-armed America’s neighbors into accepting in his first term. The threat of Section 338 tariffs gives the United States leverage to seek fresh concessions from Ottawa.
“From Carney’s perspective, you need (USMCA) to be renegotiated,” said Christopher Gundermann, a fellow in the economics program at the Center for Strategic and International Studies. “You can’t renegotiate it with a massive trade war going on.’'
But the Canadian public’s furor over Trump’s policies may limit Carney’s ability to cut a deal. Canada could retaliate again if the new 50% tariffs take effect, potentially aggravating a trade fight.
Canada’s government “cannot look like it is simply caving to the Trump administration’s demands,’’ said Daniel Béland, a political science professor at McGill University in Montreal. “Making further concessions without getting something meaningful in exchange would probably lead to a strong backlash ... The risk is for the Carney government to make Canada look weak and, therefore, even more vulnerable to future trade and geopolitical bullying on the part of the Trump administration.”
Dominic LeBlanc, Canada’s minister for U.S. trade, met with Greer on Monday. He was tight-lipped afterward.
“The work is continuing,’’ he said. “We continue to do our job.’’
____
Gillies reported from Toronto.

articles.title: Israel strikes NE. Syria's abandoned Abu al-Duhur air base
articles.body:
Israel carried out a series of airstrikes on northeastern Syria's Abu al-Duhur military air base Tuesday, according to Syrian state media and a war monitor.
The attack on the disused air base came after a recent visit to the site by a Turkish delegation.
Israel has been carrying out incursions into Syrian territory since the December 2024 overthrow of longtime ruler Bashar Assad, including sending troops into a U.N.-patrolled buffer zone that separated Israeli and Syrian forces in the Israeli-occupied Golan Heights since 1974.
It has also hit key military sites including several airfields, according to the U.K.-based war monitor, Syrian Observatory for Human Rights.
"Israeli occupation aircraft early this morning targeted the runway ... with eight strikes," Syrian state television quoted an unidentified military source as saying.
It added that "the attack resulted in material damage to the airport's infrastructure, without causing casualties."
The facility has been out of service since 2012 and is currently protected by Syrian Defense Ministry forces, a security source told Agence France-Presse (AFP), without reporting any casualties.
According to the Syrian Observatory for Human Rights, the strikes came after "a visit by a Turkish military delegation to the airfield in recent days as part of efforts to reactivate it."
Türkiye is a key ally of the new government in Damascus.
No side has claimed the strikes on the airfield and the Israeli military said "no comment" in response to an AFP inquiry about the strikes.
A U.S.-led international coalition against the Daesh terrorist group has previously carried out strikes on senior terrorist figures in the northwest.
Syria is now part of the coalition.
Israel has launched hundreds of strikes on Syria since the fall of Assad and Israeli officials have said they intend to keep forces in a "security zone" in southern Syria, where they seek a broader so-called "demilitarized zone."
Damascus has repeatedly condemned incursions in the country's south.
During a joint press conference with his French counterpart Emmanuel Macron in Damascus last month, Syrian President Ahmed al-Sharaa called for an "active French role" to halt Israeli escalations in his country.
Syrian Foreign Minister Asaad al-Shaibani also last month condemned "the continuation of Israeli military actions" and warned that "the unlawful occupation of our land beyond the 1974 line is a direct threat to the security of the region."
He demanded an "immediate and unconditional withdrawal."
But last week Israeli Defense Minister Israel Katz said that his country planned to keep troops in Syria.
Israel captured most of the Golan from Syria in the 1967 Arab-Israeli War and later annexed the areas under its control, in a move not recognized by most of the international community.
The incursions have been condemned by the United Nations chief as "violations of Syria's sovereignty and territorial integrity."
Despite tensions between the neighbors, Israel and Syria's new authorities have held several rounds of direct talks and have agreed to establish an intelligence-sharing mechanism.
Syrian President Ahmed al-Sharaa in June denied that his country sought to intervene militarily in Lebanon, where Israel is raising a separate war, after U.S. President Donald Trump suggested Damascus could get involved.
Hezbollah fought alongside Assad in the country's civil war, making al-Sharaa and the new authorities who toppled the former leader in 2024 deeply hostile to the group.
Syria's war shattered the country's infrastructure and pushed millions of people to flee internally and abroad.

articles.title: "We will be there in Ukraine's hour ‌of ⁠need": UK rejects Kremlin threats over drone supplies
articles.body:
"We will be there in Ukraine's hour of need": UK rejects Kremlin threats over drone supplies
UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham has said London will support Ukraine 100% against Russia and remain by its side "in its hour of need" after Moscow warned London of "consequences" over drone supplies to Kyiv.
Source: Reuters, as reported by European Pravda
Details: Burnham said the UK is "doing what it has long said it would do, which is to support Ukraine 100% against this illegal war" led by Russian ruler Vladimir Putin.
Quote from Burnham: "We are not fair-weather friends. We will be there in Ukraine's hour of need, and that won't change."
Details: Ukraine uses drones to carry out long-range strikes on Russian oil refineries and logistics facilities.
The UK's Ministry of Defence has not confirmed whether British-made drones have been used in these strikes.
In June, the UK said it would supply Ukraine with 150,000 drones by the end of 2026 as part of a £752 million (US$996 million) funding package.
Background:
- Russia has accused the UK of "deliberately seeking escalation" after reports in the media said British-made drones had been used in strikes on targets inside Russia.
- In late July, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy and Burnham held their first meeting aboard an aircraft carrier stationed at the British naval base in Portsmouth.
- Burnham also announced that London would provide Ukraine with technology to protect Ukrainian drones.
- In early August, the UK Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office announced an expansion of sanctions against Russia, adding 19 more entities to its sanctions list.
	
Support Ukrainska Pravda on Patreon to help us keep reporting!

articles.title: Israel strikes Syrian military airfield after Turkish delegation visit, drawing rare US rebuke
articles.body:
Israel carried out an unusual strike deep inside Syria overnight, targeting the Abu al-Duhur military airfield in the eastern Idlib countryside after a reported visit by a Turkish military delegation to the site, according to Syrian and regional reports. The attack prompted rare public criticism from U.S. special envoy for Syria Tom Barrack, who said he was “deeply concerned” and described the strikes as an “unnecessary escalation.”
Syrian military officials told Reuters that four unidentified aircraft struck the airfield, damaging runways and storage facilities. One military official and a resident living nearby said there were no fatalities. The Sabereen News agency also reported that a runway at the base had been hit.
Syrian authorities blamed Israel for the attack, which came after a prolonged period without reported IDF strikes deep inside the country. The IDF declined to comment on the reports, but a senior Israeli official later acknowledged to Fox News that Israel had carried out the operation.
The official said Jerusalem had shared “sensitive intelligence” with Washington before the strike and that the information had been passed “at the highest levels of the various agencies and bodies” in both countries.
The official also sent a message to Syrian President Ahmad al-Sharaa, saying: “He understands that he cannot operate like the previous Syrian regime. It is possible that he did not understand what was happening, or did not know.”
Barrack, however, issued an unusually pointed condemnation. In a post, he said the “confirmed” strikes represented “an unnecessary escalation that does not advance regional stability.”
He praised al-Sharaa’s government, saying Syria under his leadership “has not adopted an aggressive posture and has not maintained proxy forces.” Instead, Barrack said, Damascus had repeatedly expressed a preference for reducing tensions with Israel.
“The United States continues to believe that restraint and diplomatic engagement are the more constructive path,” he said. “We encourage all parties to prioritize reasonable dialogue over further military incidents.”
Turkey also strongly condemned the Israeli strikes on Abu al-Duhur air base, accusing Israel of violating international law and urging a tougher international response. “We call on the international community to take a more decisive stance to end Israel’s escalating aggression against Syria,” the Turkish Foreign Ministry said Tuesday.
Syrian Foreign Minister Asaad al-Shaibani also accused Israel of responsibility during a joint press conference with International Atomic Energy Agency Director General Rafael Grossi.
“We condemn the Israeli aggression, which constitutes an unjustified provocation, a violation of Syrian sovereignty and a direct threat to regional and international stability,” al-Shaibani said.
The two officials reaffirmed what they described as Syria’s sovereignty and called for an immediate end to Israeli violations. Syrian officials said Damascus was committed to becoming “a pillar of stability at the regional and international level,” while accusing Israel of pursuing a policy of “aggression and chaos.”
The Syrian Foreign Ministry later issued a separate statement explicitly blaming Israel. “Syria strongly condemns the Israeli airstrikes against Abu al-Duhur airport in Idlib province,” it said, calling the attack “unjustified aggression, a violation of Syria’s sovereignty and territorial integrity, and a dangerous escalation that threatens security and stability in the region.”
The ministry said it held Israel responsible for the escalation and called on the international community and the UN Security Council to condemn the strike.
Sources cited by the Qatari outlet Al-Araby Al-Jadeed said the Israeli attack came after a Turkish military delegation visited Abu al-Duhur to examine rehabilitation of its runway. That timing could add another layer of sensitivity to the strike amid Turkey’s growing role in postwar Syria.
Abu al-Duhur airfield lies about 27 kilometers east of Saraqib, near the village of Abu al-Duhur. Its position between the provinces of Idlib, Hama and Aleppo, close to the Syrian desert, has long given it strategic significance.
The base was considered one of northern Syria’s more prominent military installations under the previous regime. Estimates of its size vary, with some sources placing it at roughly 16 square kilometers and others at about 23 square kilometers. The facility includes several runways.
During the Syrian civil war, opposition forces captured the airfield in 2015. Forces loyal to the former Syrian regime retook it in January 2018 following a major offensive launched in late 2017 with Russian support.
The overnight attack stands out because of both its location and the diplomatic reaction it triggered. While Israel has repeatedly acted inside Syria over the years against what it described as military threats, the strike drew an unusually direct rebuke from Washington at a time when the U.S. administration is publicly urging restraint and diplomatic engagement between Jerusalem and Damascus.

articles.title: Putin hosts Myanmar’s leader for talks on deepening their relationship
articles.body:
Putin hosts Myanmar’s leader for talks on deepening their relationship
MOSCOW (AP) — President Vladimir Putin on Tuesday hosted the head of Myanmar’s military-backed government, who visited Russia on a trip to boost their cooperation.
Speaking at the start of the talks with President Min Aung Hlaing, Putin noted both countries have cooperated on foreign policy and security issues and developed economic projects.
They have held joint military drills and developed plans for Russia to build a nuclear power plant, a seaport, oil refineries and other facilities in Myanmar.
The visit is the latest in a series of trips by Min Aung Hlaing to foreign countries, including neighboring China, India, Laos and Thailand as he seeks to strengthen international recognition and regain diplomatic standing with other countries.
Despite the visits, Myanmar has remained largely isolated internationally since the military seized power from the elected government of Aung San Suu Kyi in February 2021.
Western nations have imposed economic and political sanctions in response to the takeover by the military, which he led, and its violent repression of the opposition, which has seen the deaths of thousands of civilians and given rise to a civil war.
Russia has defended Min Aung Hlaing’s military government in international forums while Myanmar’s ruling generals have generally supported Moscow’s foreign policy agenda.
During Tuesday’s talks, Min Aung Hlaing thanked Putin for his political support and emphasized that Myanmar has remained a reliable partner.
Russia, along with China, is a major supporter and arms supplier to Myanmar. Russian-made fighter jets are used in attacks on territory under the control of ethnic minority groups, including many allied with pro-democracy resistance forces.
Russia’s Economic Development Minister Maxim Reshetnikov told reporters that Moscow stands ready to increase supplies of oil products, fertilizers and equipment to Myanmar and boost imports of agricultural products and textiles from the country.
The trip marks Min Aung Hlaing’s seventh visit to Russia. Min Aung Hlaing previously met Putin on the sidelines of Moscow’s World Atomic Week Forum in September. Putin has never visited Myanmar.
Min Aung Hlaing was inaugurated in April following a general election judged by United Nations experts and rights groups to be neither free nor fair. Critics dismissed the polls, held in phases in December and January, as a sham designed to consolidate the military’s grip on power while ostensibly restoring civilian rule.

articles.title: Iran says Hormuz stays closed until US meets its demands
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Iran says Hormuz stays closed until US meets its demands
Iran has set out a series of conditions for reopening the Strait of Hormuz, including the lifting of US sanctions and the release of frozen Iranian funds, a day after a deadline for Tehran and Washington to reach a final agreement expired without a deal.
Iranian parliament speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf said on Tuesday that Tehran would not reopen the strategic waterway until Washington fulfilled commitments Iran says were included in a memorandum of understanding reached in June.
"The strait will not be opened unless America fulfils its commitments contained in the memorandums of understanding, including lifting the blockade, releasing frozen funds, lifting oil sanctions, ending threats and military operations on all fronts, and the other conditions America committed to," Ghalibaf said.
His remarks came a day after a 60-day deadline for Iran and the United States to reach a final agreement expired, leaving the two sides locked in a dispute over the waterway at the centre of the nearly six-month war.
Speaking during a virtual public session of parliament, Ghalibaf warned that Iran was "ready to inflict a greater defeat than the previous one on the enemy if it seeks to attack us".
He said Iran was acting under instructions from Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei, using both the "power of logic" and the "logic of power" to force what he called a "delusional America" to deliver what Tehran considers the rights of the Iranian people.
Ghalibaf also accused Iran's adversaries of shifting their focus towards economic pressure and attempts to exploit divisions inside the country after, he claimed, failing to defeat Tehran militarily or diplomatically.
"The enemy, in its new plan, seeks economic pressure and the destruction of the country's cohesion," he said.
He warned that any individual or institution that weakened national unity through its statements, conduct or decisions would be serving the enemy's objectives, whether intentionally or otherwise.
Ghalibaf said Iran had used the period created by the memorandum of understanding, including the easing of the blockade and the ceasefire, to strengthen its economic resilience and rebuild its defence capabilities.
He claimed Iranian authorities had information suggesting that their adversaries were looking for opportunities to foment unrest and combine it with military operations, including assassinations and separatist activity, alongside what he described as "cognitive warfare".
The parliament speaker also suggested Iran's adversaries could seek to exploit government measures intended to reduce petrol consumption.
While acknowledging that Iranians' economic grievances were legitimate and saying he respected political and social criticism, Ghalibaf argued that the country was at a moment that required unity.
Iran says Hormuz remains under its control
The deputy commander of Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps, Major General Mostafa Izadi, separately underlined Tehran's position on the Strait of Hormuz, saying control of the waterway remained "entirely at the discretion of Iran's sons".
"The enemy does not know what to do," Izadi was quoted as saying by Iran's Fars news agency.
He described the strait as equivalent in strategic value to "nuclear power", pointing to its impact on global energy, agriculture and industry.
The comments reinforce Iran's insistence on retaining leverage over the waterway, which has emerged as the central obstacle to efforts to turn the ceasefire into a lasting settlement.
Araghchi says US failed to force Iranian surrender
Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi, meanwhile, said on Tuesday that US efforts to force Iran into "unconditional surrender" during the war had failed.
Araghchi said the US administration had entered the war seeking Iran's complete surrender, before subsequently pursuing regime change, the partition of the country and efforts to arm groups inside Iranian cities and western regions.
He said those efforts had also failed.
The United States, Araghchi claimed, "rushed" to seek negotiations shortly after the war began, despite initially demanding Tehran's unconditional surrender.
Iran initially rejected a ceasefire and continued fighting until the other side became convinced of the need to accept a truce and negotiate on Tehran's terms, he said.
Araghchi said the events would eventually be recorded "in detail in history", describing an exchange of multi-point proposals that culminated in an agreement based on an Iranian proposal for a ceasefire in April.
Months of negotiations followed, lasting longer than the war itself, before the two sides signed a memorandum of understanding on 18 June, he said.
Araghchi said foreign diplomats had told him that most of the memorandum's provisions favoured Iran, while only a small portion benefited the other side.
He claimed this was why the agreement began to be violated less than two weeks after it was signed, accusing Israel of being its most determined opponent and of seeking to prevent both its conclusion and implementation.
Monday marked the deadline for Iran and the United States to reach a final agreement under the Qatar- and Pakistan-mediated memorandum of understanding intended to bring the war to an end.
The agreement gave the two sides 60 days to negotiate a broader settlement covering issues including the future of Iran's nuclear programme and US sanctions on Tehran.
But the memorandum, which called for an immediate and permanent cessation of military operations on all fronts, quickly ran into difficulties as the two sides clashed over control of the Strait of Hormuz.

articles.title: Taiwan launches first live-fire exercise with first-person view drones
articles.body:
Taiwan launches first live-fire exercise with first-person view drones
The island’s military is working to learn the lessons of the Ukraine war and boost its asymmetric defences against the PLA
Taiwan’s army has for the first time used first-person view (FPV) drones against armoured vehicles in a live-fire exercise, adopting tactics pioneered during the Ukraine war to strengthen its asymmetric capabilities against the People’s Liberation Army.
The exercise on Monday highlighted efforts to broaden strike options beyond traditional firepower such as rocket systems and heavy artillery.
The Army Unmanned Systems Training Command brought together six units from the military’s artillery commands, Marine Corps and Military Police for the exercise.
Under simulated battlefield conditions, operators flew FPV drones carrying armour-piercing warheads against decommissioned tanks and armoured ammunition carriers.
FPV drones – which stream real-time video directly to a pair of goggles worn by the pilot – are usually designed to be more manoeuvrable and acrobatic than other drones, allowing greater accuracy in combat.
The drones conducted frontal and flanking strikes in both single-drone and coordinated two-drone attacks, according to the Youth Daily News, a defence ministry-affiliated newspaper based in Taipei.

articles.title: Wang Yi heads to Seoul as Trump cuts South Korea drills, opening door for China
articles.body:
Wang Yi heads to Seoul as Trump cuts South Korea drills, opening door for China
Experts say US decision causes disquiet among regional partners and hands China a strategic opening to dilute US regional partnerships
The US president posted his decision to social media on Sunday, raising questions about the durability of Washington’s security commitments in a region increasingly defined by competition with Beijing.
He offered several rationales, including cost-saving considerations, a goodwill gesture towards North Korea, and dissatisfaction with Seoul’s refusal to join the US in the war against Iran.
Observers said such moves threatened to damage alliance coordination, causing disquiet among regional partners and handing China a strategic opening to dilute America’s network of regional partnerships.
He added that he had ordered the US defence secretary to “substantially reduce” the drills, citing Seoul’s reluctance to support America’s efforts towards the “denuclearisation of the Islamic Republic of Iran”.
As Seoul and other US partners navigate the latest shocks, Wang will begin a two-day trip to Seoul on Wednesday, his first bilateral exchange trip in five years.

articles.title: New satellite imagery shows a caved-in roof at Russia’s only Soyuz rocket-assembly plant
articles.body:
Satellite imagery shows the damage Ukraine's Flamingo missiles inflicted on Russia's main rocket-assembly plant, the Ukrainian Telegram channel Exilenova+ reported on 18 August. The overhead photo show a collapsed roof section over a key hall at the Progress Rocket Space Center in Samara, a Russian city about 900 km from the war zone in Ukraine. It puts a measurable figure on damage Kyiv had until now only claimed.
The satellite photo centers the damage on building 106A, Exilenova+ said. Crews there wire the rockets' control systems, cabling and instrument bays. The imagery shows two missile hits on that hall, the channel reported.
The collapsed roof section runs 85 meters long and 35 meters wide. Ukraine struck the plant on 15 August with its home-built Flamingo cruise missiles, which President Volodymyr Zelenskyy confirmed at the time.
Reported Flamingo strike hits Samara industrial area housing factory that builds rockets for Russia’s Starlink rival
A rocket hall with no domestic replacement
Progress is the only plant in Russia that serially assembles the Soyuz-2 rocket family, used to launch military reconnaissance and targeting satellites, Exilenova+ noted.
The plant also lofts the Rassvet satellites built by Bureau 1440, Russia's answer to Starlink. The country has no full alternative to the Samara site, they added. Next to building 106A stands 106B, the complex's final-assembly hall.
Ukraine's Fire Point company builds the Flamingo, a long-range cruise missile. Its growing reach lets Kyiv strike defense and space plants far from the front. Overhead imagery has exposed earlier Flamingo damage deep inside Russia.

articles.title: Trump’s approval rating has fallen to its lowest point in his presidency
articles.body:
A poll of voters shows that US President Donald Trump’s approval rating has fallen to its lowest point in his presidency, with most Americans worried about the protracted war with Iran, Reuters reports.
In a four-day Reuters/Ipsos poll, only 33% of respondents rated Trump’s performance in the White House positively, while 64% rated it poorly. In early August, 35% of those surveyed described the president’s work as successful. Now, support has reached the level it was at the lowest point during Trump’s previous term.
After returning to the White House in 2025, when slightly less than half of the country’s voters supported Trump’s election, his popularity has fallen significantly after the United States, together with its ally Israel, launched strikes on Iran. The conflict has halted shipping in the Strait of Hormuz, a major oil and gas export route from the Persian Gulf, and has sent fuel prices soaring, which is now being felt by American households. It is also affecting Republicans’ prospects in the midterm elections due in November.
Trump’s campaign was based on promises to control inflation and avoid engaging in a protracted war, and he initially promised that the war in Iran would last only a few weeks. However, Iran has proven to be more powerful than Trump thought, and traffic in the Strait of Hormuz has not yet returned to normal. About 80% of Americans (87% of Democrats and 71% of Republicans) believe that the US involvement in the war in Iran will continue for a long time.
Only 16% of those surveyed believe that the conflict could be ended in the coming weeks.
Trump said at a political event on the 14th of August that a small increase in gas prices is a small price to pay for not having a “very evil country” with nuclear weapons. That is also the president’s main argument for war with Iran. Since the start of hostilities, Trump has vacillated between threats of escalation and assumptions that a peace deal is inevitable and close. Only one in five Americans believe the war has been worth it.
Concerns about war and gas prices have Republicans worried about their chances of defending their slim majority in the House of Representatives; the reins of power in the Senate could also go to the Democrats.
A Reuters/Ipsos poll showed that for the first time in a decade, voters believe that Democrats are better at managing the economy. 38% of voters believe that Democrats are better at handling the economy, while 35% of voters think that Republicans are better at handling economic issues.
Meanwhile, the Republican approach to immigration remains more popular than the policies implemented by the Democrats, but Republicans are losing ground in this area as well, as the number of deadly clashes has increased, mass arrests are increasingly causing widespread resonance, and the situation in migrant detention centers is causing concern.

articles.title: 10 new Russian bases for drones could threaten not only Ukraine - ISW
articles.body:
10 new Russian bases for drones could threaten not only Ukraine - ISW
Kyiv • UNN
Russia is building new launch sites for attack drones along its border with Ukraine and Belarus, which could threaten not only Ukraine. ISW analysts warn of possible threat to NATO territory.
Russia's expansion of launch sites for Russian attack drones along the border with Ukraine and Belarus may threaten not only Ukraine, the Institute for the Study of War (ISW) said in a new report dated August 17, UNN reports.
Details
"Russia is expanding launch sites for its long-range attack drones along the border with Ukraine and Belarus, likely to intensify strikes against Ukraine and possibly NATO," the ISW report says.
On August 16, The Telegraph reported that Russia had built 59 new drone launch facilities at 10 different locations along its border with Ukraine and Belarus, and that each base could accommodate more than 1,000 drones. The Telegraph cited an analysis by a drone intelligence firm showing that around 20 of the new launch facilities are of significant length, indicating that Russian forces may use them to launch Geran-4 and Geran-5 jet-powered attack drones, which can fly ranges of 450 to 850 kilometers and 950 to 1,000 kilometers, respectively.
"Russia is likely building these additional launch sites in western Russia to increase its ability to launch larger long-range drone salvos as part of Russia's regular strikes across Ukraine. Russia is also likely seeking to use Geran-4 and Geran-5 jet-powered drones for deeper strikes in western Ukraine, using the drones' greater speed and survivability to penetrate Ukrainian air defenses," the ISW report says.
"Russia is also likely moving its drone launch sites to western Russia in an attempt to protect Russian drone infrastructure from Ukrainian drones," analysts noted.
As noted, "for example, Ukrainian forces successfully struck Russian drone launch sites near occupied Donetsk, so the creation of alternative launch sites farther inside Russia could improve their survivability."
"Russia may also be preparing to use its Rassvet satellite constellation (the Russian version of Starlink), using the new launch sites, which could allow Russian forces to conduct precision strikes against Ukraine's rear-area systems and air defense systems from different directions," the report states.
"The new Russian drone launch bases could also support future Russian strike packages against NATO if the Kremlin decides to do so, as the bases would allow for an increased volume of salvos, while the launch stations would provide the drones with operational range over NATO territory," ISW noted.

articles.title: Ukraine says 10 people killed in Russian missile strike on Kharkiv region
articles.body:
Elena Teslova and Burc Eruygur
18 August 2026•Update: 18 August 2026
- Russian authorities yet to comment on attack
 
 Ukrainian officials said on Tuesday that at least 10 people were killed and 18 others wounded in a Russian missile strike in the country's northeastern Kharkiv region.
 
In a statement on US social media company X, Zelenskyy said the strike hit an area in the settlement of Pechenihy where a post office and shops were located, surrounded by residential buildings.
 
“As of now, 10 people are known to have been killed,” he said.
 
Emergency services extinguished a fire at the site and continued working there to establish the circumstances of the incident, he added.
 
Zelenskyy added that Ukraine would respond to the attack, and called on its international partners to increase pressure on Russia.
 
Separately, Kharkiv Governor Oleh Synyehubov said on Telegram that eight people were injured in the attack, which he described as a missile strike. He later updated the number of those injured to 18.
 
Russian authorities have yet to comment on the attack.
 
Moscow and Kyiv have increasingly targeted each other's logistics centers as well as port and energy infrastructure in recent months.
 
Both sides deny deliberately targeting civilian infrastructure, maintaining that their strikes are directed at military targets or facilities linked to military activities.

articles.title: Kiev deliberately disrupts dialogue with IAEA on Zaporozhye NPP, local politician says
articles.body:
MELITOPOL, August 18. /TASS/. The Kiev regime intentionally obstructs dialogue regarding the Zaporozhye Nuclear Power Plant (ZNPP), particularly efforts involving the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA). This obstruction appears aimed at preventing any resolution that might limit Kiev’s ability to leverage the plant as a tool of blackmail against Russia. In line with this strategy, Kiev barred IAEA Director General Rafael Grossi from visiting the ZNPP, as reported by Anton Bibarov-Gosudarev, Chairman of the Zaporozhye Region’s Civic Chamber, to TASS.
"Ukraine shows no genuine interest in engaging in dialogue about the Zaporozhye NPP," Bibarov-Gosudarev stated. "Instead, maintaining tension serves to hinder the peaceful development of nuclear energy in the region for as long as possible. To this end, they are prepared not only to attack infrastructure and threaten civilian lives but also to escalate provocations, such as today’s attack on a public transportation stop. Kiev’s manipulation of the ZNPP as a tool for blackmail makes the disruption of Grossi’s visit part of a broader plan to prevent any resolution of the situation surrounding the plant."
The provocation by Kiev exemplifies its dismissive attitude toward the IAEA and other international institutions, the agency’s source emphasized. Nonetheless, the IAEA’s patience underscores the influence Kiev’s sponsors wield over the organization.
Russian Foreign Ministry Spokeswoman Maria Zakharova condemned Kiev’s sabotage of Grossi’s scheduled visit to Energodar on August 20-21, describing it as "yet another reckless move." She pointed out that all arrangements for the trip had been thoroughly coordinated in advance by the IAEA Secretariat and Russia, with Moscow providing security guarantees that satisfied the Agency. Despite this, Kiev cynically threatened Grossi, explicitly stating it could not ensure his safety when entering the ZNPP through Russian-controlled territory, Zakharova added.
Earlier, on Tuesday at approximately 6:00 a.m. Moscow time (3:00 a.m. GMT), Ukrainian drones targeted an area near a bus stop in Energodar - a town adjacent to the ZNPP - where civilians were waiting for transportation. The attack resulted in one death and 17 injuries, three of which are classified as moderate. Medical personnel report the condition of the remaining victims as satisfactory. The Russian Investigative Committee has launched a criminal investigation into the incident.

articles.title: 637 Drones Target Moscow Region as Wildberries Warehouses Suffer Billions in Losses
articles.body:
Moscow and the region faced one of the largest drone attacks of the war overnight as Russian authorities reported over 600 Ukrainian drones targeting the capital and surrounding region, while a Wildberries warehouse caught fire and power infrastructure was damaged.
From the evening of Aug. 17 through the morning of Aug. 18, 637 Ukrainian drones were launched toward the Russian capital, Moscow Mayor Sergei Sobyanin reported.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
According to Sobyanin, at least 180 of the drones were shot down directly over the region. Moscow Region Governor Andrei Vorobyov, meanwhile, reported the interception of more than 150 drones in Bogorodskoye, Ramenskoye, Pavlovsky Posad, Orekhovo-Zuyevo, Voskresensk, Stupino, Kolomna and Elektrostal.
In Pavlovsky Posad, the roof of an apartment building caught fire, prompting the evacuation of residents. No injuries were reported there, Vorobyov said.
In the Ramenskoye District, a drone crashed onto a private home, injuring a 10-year-old girl. Two other people were injured by falling drone debris in Kolomna and Bogorodsky District, according to the governor.
One of the facilities affected by the attack was a Wildberries warehouse in Bogorodsky, where a fire broke out. The company said its employees were evacuated and that the fire was “quickly dealt with.” It added that no goods were damaged.
Vorobyov also reported a fire at a retail pavilion near the Globus shopping center in Kolomna. The blaze damaged a registry office, a store and the windows of a residential building on Sovetskaya Square.
Britain Hits Back at Russian Threats Over Ukraine’s Use of British Drones
The attack also damaged the regional power grid. Mosoblenergo reported that 109 transformer substations were knocked out, leaving more than 5,000 customers and 46 socially important facilities without electricity in the Likino-Dulyovo and Orekhovo-Zuyevo urban districts.
Mosoblenergo said it planned to restore power within two hours.
Wildberries warehouses repeatedly targeted
The latest incident comes after another major drone attack on the Moscow region on Aug. 16, when Sobyanin reported that about 600 drones were heading toward the region. Russian authorities said 201 of them were shot down over the Moscow region.
The repeated attacks have also affected Wildberries, one of Russia’s largest e-commerce companies. A satellite image posted by the Ukrainian Telegram monitoring channel Exilenova+ showed that a Wildberries warehouse in the village of Koledino near Podolsk was completely destroyed in a drone attack on Aug. 16.
Msk1 reported that firefighters battled the blaze from both the ground and the air, with four helicopters deployed to extinguish it. Despite those efforts, the facility was reportedly “reduced to rubble.”
The destroyed complex covered an estimated 230,000-250,000 square meters, according to different estimates. It was reportedly Wildberries’ largest hub and one of the key nodes in its logistics network.
Data Insight analyst Sergey Semko said that goods worth an estimated 78 billion rubles ($918 million) were destroyed in the fire at the Koledino warehouse. According to Semko, the facility had enabled Wildberries to maintain delivery times of one to two days across Moscow and the surrounding region.
Following the previous attack on Koledino, Ukrainian drone manufacturer Fire Point said strikes against such facilities weaken Russia’s economic potential by disrupting supply chains and causing losses for major companies.
The Koledino area was previously targeted on July 28, when a fire broke out at the nearby Koledino3Pl logistics complex following a drone strike.
Billions in losses
Ukraine began targeting Wildberries infrastructure on July 18, according to Verstka. Over the following month, at least 22 of the marketplace’s warehouses were hit, with 19 reportedly significantly or completely destroyed.
Among the facilities affected were major logistics centers in Elektrostal near Moscow and Aleksin in the Tula region.
The reported damage represents about 2.395 million square meters of warehouse space, or 43% of Wildberries’ total warehouse capacity of approximately 5.6 million square meters, according to Verstka.
The month-long attacks on Wildberries facilities reportedly killed at least 14 people and injured more than 100.
As of Aug. 14, Data Insight estimated the value of goods destroyed in fires at affected Wildberries warehouses at 445-507 billion rubles ($5.24-5.96 billion). The Association of Suppliers of Goods for Trading on Electronic Platforms (APTEP) put the figure even higher, at 600-700 billion rubles ($7.06-8.24 billion).
Data Insight estimated that Wildberries itself suffered 147-223 billion rubles ($1.7–2.6 billion) in direct losses.
The damage has raised concerns about the wider impact on Russia’s e-commerce sector and the thousands of sellers who depend on Wildberries’ logistics network. Russia may not have sufficient funds to compensate affected sellers, according to a source close to the Kremlin cited by Reuters.
The source said the damage to Wildberries, which controls roughly half of Russia’s e-commerce market, represented a “serious blow to the economy.”
“There will be a wave of bankruptcies. No one has the kind of money to support sellers,” the source predicted.
The Ukrainian Defense Ministry said on Aug. 16 that recent operations had disabled seven of Wildberries’ 10 largest logistics centers. The strikes are part of a sustained Ukrainian campaign against the Russian e-commerce giant, which accounts for about 10% of Russia’s retail sales.
On Aug. 10-11, Ukraine’s Main Intelligence Directorate (HUR) also targeted Wildberries’ digital infrastructure, disrupting customer services and payments.
Kyiv says Wildberries is a legitimate military target because the platform sells goods used by Russian forces. While the company denies supplying the military, reports say dual-use items, including FPV drones and fiber-optic cables, were available on the marketplace in early August.

articles.title: US calls on Poland to transfer Patriot missiles to Kyiv, no decision made yet – Tomczyk
articles.body:
Poland has not yet made a decision regarding the transfer of PAC-3 missiles for the Patriot system to Ukraine, stated Deputy Minister of National Defence Cezary Tomczyk.
"No decisions have been made on this matter," Tomczyk said on Polish Radio 24. He recalled that Poland has so far supported Kyiv with several such missiles "out of the hundreds we have."
The Deputy Minister assured that Poland is safe. "Polish stocks are full, secure, and being replenished," Tomczyk added.
"Ukraine’s main need today is protection against ballistic missiles. Cities like Kyiv and Lviv are subjected to attacks by Russia daily. It is obvious that Ukraine is asking its Western partners for the transfer or the opportunity to purchase missiles for Patriot systems," Tomczyk said. He emphasized that Poland receives most of the calls from the United States.
"It is the Supreme Allied Commander Europe of US Forces, General Hrynkevych, as well as the US administration, who very often convey these appeals to the Polish government to transfer missiles for Patriot systems when possible," Tomczyk acknowledged.
He stressed that any decision on transferring the missiles must be made at the highest level. "First, the Minister of National Defence submits recommendations, and then the Council of Ministers makes the decision," Tomczyk outlined the procedure.
When asked about the possibility of launching Patriot missile production in Poland, Tomczyk replied: "That is the plan." "We are currently at a very favorable moment in terms of our relations with the Americans," he said. Tomczyk noted that a contract to build a service center for Patriot missiles has already been signed, stating that this is an intermediate step before production becomes possible.
Tomczyk remarked that US President Donald Trump, following his initial statement regarding production in Ukraine, "either abandoned it or put a major question mark over it." "Let’s be frank, during a war in Ukraine, producing this type of system is practically impossible," Tomczyk said. "I think there is a great opportunity here for Poland as well," he added.

articles.title: 650 participants from 24 countries: Ukraine brings its battle-tested drone-defense experience to NATO’s Baltic Trust 2026 exercise
articles.body:
Ukraine brought the world's most battle-tested counter-drone experience to a NATO exercise. From 3 to 14 August, Ukraine took part in NATO's Baltic Trust 2026 exercise in Latvia, which focused on countering drones and other threats posed by uncrewed aerial systems, the General Staff reported.
The exercise responds to a mounting Russian threat against NATO's Baltic flank. Russia has probed the alliance's eastern edge so aggressively that NATO scrambled over the Baltic, jumping more than 250% in July.
Also, Moscow has increasingly launched drones on the Baltic States. Even on 14 August, the final day of the drill, a NATO fighter shot down a drone over Latvia after Russian electronic warfare pushed it off course, the second Baltic drone incursion that week. Baltic Trust 2026 was NATO's answer: about 650 participants from 24 countries building the counter-drone defenses that the threat demands.
The exercise tested systems working together
Baltic Trust focused on integration, not single technologies. Soldiers, specialists, and industry representatives jointly tested new technological solutions in conditions close to a modern operational environment, the General Staff said.
The core was whether the pieces work as one system. Participants checked how detection tools, command-and-control systems, and counter-drone measures can exchange data, form a common operational picture, and enable coordinated response.
Ukraine's experience is the draw
Ukraine's participation carries particular weight in this field. No NATO member has faced the scale of drone attack Ukraine confronts nightly, and its forces have built and continually adapt the detection, interception, and electronic-warfare methods that down Russian drones by the tens of thousands.
That makes Ukraine a source of hard-won practical knowledge for allies still preparing for threats Ukraine already lives with. Bringing Ukrainian experience into a NATO drill turns the country's battlefield lessons into shared allied capability, on exactly the drone warfare the alliance is scrambling to counter on its eastern flank.
The exercise builds collective defense
Baltic Trust served NATO's broader readiness. Jointly testing and integrating such solutions helps turn technological innovation into practical capabilities that strengthen readiness and collective defense.
Previously, Russia's Foreign Intelligence Service Head Sergey Naryshkin accused NATO of escalating military activity near Russia’s borders. He warned that Poland and the Baltic states would be the first to suffer in the event of a war between Moscow and the Alliance.

articles.title: Poland “99% sure” fugitive opposition politician is in pro-Russian breakaway region of Moldova
articles.body:
Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work!
Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support.
Poland’s prime minister, Donald Tusk, says that they are “99% certain” that fugitive opposition politician Marcin Romanowski is in Transnistria, a breakaway region of Moldova that has close links to Russia.
Last week, judicial authorities in Poland confirmed that they had received a letter purportedly from Romanowski, who is wanted in Poland for 11 alleged crimes committed while he served as a deputy justice minister in the former national-conservative Law and Justice (PiS) government.
In the document, Romanowski claimed to be in Transnistria and requested safe passage back to Poland. However, as the authenticity of the letter had not been confirmed, some media outlets speculated that the politician may not, in fact, be in Transnistria.
Meanwhile, the Moldovan authorities quickly announced that they had no record of Romanowski travelling to Transnistria, which is a landlocked territory that only has borders with Moldova and Ukraine and operates no commercial passenger flights.
A former government minister who fled criminal charges in Poland appears to be in Transnistria, a breakaway region of Moldova that has close links with Russia.
Marcin Romanowski's whereabouts have been unknown since he left Hungary earlier this year https://t.co/MPWroFVbMe
— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) August 13, 2026
Speaking on Tuesday morning, Przemysław Nowak, spokesman for Poland’s National Prosecutor’s Office, said they have “still not confirmed” the veracity of Romanowski’s claim to be in Transnistria, reported broadcaster RMF.
However, shortly afterwards, speaking ahead of a meeting of his cabinet on Tuesday, Tusk said he wanted to address the issue given there has been “a great deal of speculation and misinformation regarding Mr Romanowski and his whereabouts”.
“I can say that the intelligence services of other countries in the region with which we cooperate have confirmed to us the information that Mr Romanowski is 99% certain – I say that just in case – to be in Transnistria, in Tiraspol,” he continued, referring to the capital of the breakaway region.
"Pan Romanowski znajduje się na 99 procent w Naddniestrzu. Chyba nie trzeba tu komentarzy"
Donald Tusk podczas posiedzenia rządu ⤵️ pic.twitter.com/muVQVKrOTs
— tvp.info 🇵🇱 (@tvp_info) August 18, 2026
Transnistria is a narrow strip of land in eastern Moldova that sought to become a separate state in the early 1990s as the Soviet Union collapsed, fighting a war between 1990 and 1992.
Today, the territory, which has a population of around 360,000, operates as a de facto state but is not recognised by any other country. Its flag and national emblem feature the Soviet hammer and sickle.
Transnistria has close ties with Russia, which maintains a military “peacekeeping” force there. Various experts and former intelligence officials have noted that it would be impossible for Romanowski to enter without Russia’s approval.
The fact that Romanowski appears to be hiding there has led to criticism of PiS, the party Romanowski still technically serves as an MP and which publicly takes a strongly anti-Russian position.
“If it is true that [Romanowski] is in Transnistria, a republic not recognised by anyone, de facto controlled 100% by Russia, then it must have happened through and with the participation of Russia,” said defence minister Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz last week.
“Escaping under the Russian umbrella is the worst possible thing, because not only are they cowardly, but they are also joining the enemy of Poland,” he added.
In his remarks today, Tusk said that Romanowski’s likely presence in Transnistria “speaks for itself regarding not only Mr Romanowski but the entire political group that covered up for and benefited from such people, and continues to cover up for them”.
PiS politicians have largely avoided commenting, noting that it has not been confirmed that Romanowski is in Transnistria. However, deputy leader Przemysław Czarnek last week admitted that, if Romanowski did trael there, he would have “crossed a line”.
Nie wyprzedzajmy faktów – powiedział poseł PiS Zbigniew Kuźmiuk, pytany, czy Marcin Romanowski może zostać zawieszony w partii.https://t.co/IQzuS8Ad7O
— tvn24 (@tvn24) August 14, 2026
Romanowski served as a deputy justice minister in the former PiS government from 2019 until 2023, when the party lost power to a new ruling coalition led by Tusk.
In 2024, prosecutors announced that they wanted to charge him with 11 crimes, including participating in an organised criminal group and using crime as a source of income. However, he instead fled to Hungary, where he was granted asylum by the then-government of Viktor Orbán, a PiS ally.
When Orbán lost power earlier this year, his successor, Péter Magyar, promised to extradite both Romanowski and Zbigniew Ziobro, the former PiS justice minister who had also fled criminal charges in Poland and been granted asylum by Orbán.
However, as Magyar was sworn in as the new prime minister, Ziobro fled to the United States, where he remains, and Romanowski disappeared, leading to months of speculation as to his whereabouts. Both politicians deny the accusations against them and claim to be victims of political persecution by Tusk’s government.
Poland has formally asked the US to detain and extradite former justice minister @ZiobroPL, who faces multiple criminal charges.
He denies wrongdoing and calls the case political revengehttps://t.co/BXdQgWm61q
— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 27, 2026
In his comments on Tuesday morning, Nowak said that prosecutors had found “no grounds whatsoever” to approve Romanowski’s request for safe passage to Poland.
He noted that “the suspect has evaded legal proceedings, questioned the legality of the authorities’ actions, left Poland and then Hungary to avoid arrest, and publicly declared his lack of intention to return to the country due to the ongoing criminal proceedings against him”.
Polish prosecutors are still, however, attempting to confirm Romanowski’s whereabouts and secure his extradition to Poland to face justice. He is subject to a European Arrest Warrant. However, that applies only in EU countries, and Moldova is not a member of the bloc.

Daniel Tilles is editor-in-chief of Notes from Poland. He has written on Polish affairs for a wide range of publications, including Foreign Policy, POLITICO Europe, EUobserver and Dziennik Gazeta Prawna.

At least 10 people were killed and eight wounded in a strike on Pechenigy, in Ukraine's Kharkiv region, the local governor said Tuesday, as 620 drones targeted the Moscow region overnight, Russian officials said, with several people wounded and buildings struck.
